Indeed, if the previous day the vein had been roasted in the same furnace, it will heat more quickly; if not roasted, it will heat more slowly. The furnace and the crucible, if they are not heated before the vein to be roasted is put in, will cause damage to the metals. For if the dust, from which both are made, was humid in a hot season, or frozen in winter, both will break at once with the metals and other things, and like thunder, produce a loud sound, and thus be dispersed without great danger to men. Then the master should throw in the charge into the furnace: when melted, it flows out from the mouth into the crucible: then he should close the mouth with clay, with which the dust is mixed with charcoal: and this he should place with his hand on a smooth, thick wooden rod, with five fingers wide, two palms high: the handle of which should be three feet long. Then, with a hook, he should draw out the charge from the crucible: and if he is roasting a vein of gold or silver, he should put a hundred pounds of lead upon it; if it is a poor vein, half that amount: for much lead is needed for the former, and little for the latter. Then he should put lead on top, so that it melts: then he should do everything carefully and in a certain order, and throw it into the furnace, first a quantity of bread, made from the roasted pyrites, as much as is needed for roasting the vein: then the vein, with the froth of silver and molybdena, and stones which easily melt with fire, of the second kind, as much as two handfuls can hold: then as many charcoal, as the handful of wooden leaves can hold: finally the charge: the furnace, now filled with these things, will slowly roast the vein: but he should not put it too close to the back wall of the next furnace, lest the spirit be hindered by the smoke near the nostrils, and the fire burn less brightly. The master, indeed, should slowly pour water into each furnace, so that the charcoal becomes wet, so that the very thin parts of the veins, which otherwise are stirred by the bellows' breath and the fire's heat, and are carried away with the smoke, may adhere to them. But because the nature of the veins to be roasted is different, the roasters must prepare the fire now high, now low, and the pipe, in which the nostrils of the bellows are placed, sometimes very steep, sometimes not so steep: and the master should now inspire a gentle, now a strong breath into the furnace. For indeed, to veins which heat and melt quickly, the roasters need a low fire, a pipe placed not too steep, and a gentle breath from the bellows; on the contrary, to those which heat and melt slowly, a high fire, a pipe placed very steep, and a strong breath from the bellows: and even for these, the furnace itself must be very hot, and in which the charge has already been put in, or bread made from pyrites, or stones which easily melt with fire, cooked: for if the veins are not placed in the fire of the furnace, they block the mouth and almost suffocate it: which also happens often with small metallic particles, which, while the veins are being washed, settle down. Great bellows must also have wide nostrils: for if they are narrow, a large and strong breath is too tightly and sharply inspired into the furnace: from which the melted material cools down, and the smoke gathers around the nostrils,

He who is able to temper the four elements is certainly always held in the number of the excellent roasters. The master, indeed, pouring water little by little into both parts of the furnace, should moisten the coals, so that the thinnest parts of the veins, which otherwise would be carried away with the sawdust and the force of the fires and lifted with the smoke, may adhere to them. [context] Sanguification, too, which is entitled the second digestion,
is perfect before the first, or chylification, which takes place in the stomach, is begun. The excrementitious products of the first and second digestions, namely, excrement in the intestines, urine and bile in the urinary and gall bladder, are contemporaneous with the existence of the concocting organs themselves. Lastly, not only is there a soul or vital principle present in the vegetative part, but even before this there is inherent mind, foresight, and understanding, which from the very commencement to the being and perfect formation of the chick, dispose and order and take up all things requisite, moulding them in the new being, with consummate art, into the form and likeness of its parents.

In reference to this subject of family likeness, we may be permitted to inquire as to the reason why the offspring should at one time bear a stronger resemblance to the father, at another to the mother, and, at a third, to progenitors, both maternal and paternal, further removed? particularly in cases where at one bout, and at the same moment, several ova are fecundated. And this too is a remarkable fact, that virtues and vices, marks and moles, and even particular dispositions to disease are transmitted by parents to their offspring; and that while some inherit in this way, all do not. Among our poultry some are courageous, and pugnaciously inclined, and will sooner die than yield and flee from an adversary; their descendants, once or twice removed, however, unless they have come of equally well-bred parents, gradually lose this quality; according to the adage, "the brave are begotten by the brave." In various other species of animals, and particularly in the human family, a certain nobility of race is observed; numerous qualities, in fact, both of mind and body, are derived by hereditary descent.

I have frequently wondered how it should happen that the offspring, mixed in so many particulars of its structure or constitution, with the stamp of both parents so obviously upon it, in so many parts, should still escape all mixture in the organs of generation; that it should so uniformly prove either male or female, so very rarely an hermaphrodite.

Lastly, many things are present before they appear, and some are begun among the very first which are completed among the very last, such as the eyes, the organs of generation, and the beak.

[context] the other, of those bodies which
shun and abhor flame, as all salts. For we find that if salts are thrown into the fire, their aqueous spirit bursts out with a crackling noise, before flame is caught; which is the case also, though in a milder degree, with the stiffer kinds of leaves: the aqueous part escaping before the oily catches fire. But this is best seen in quicksilver, which is not inaptly called mineral water. For quicksilver, without bursting into flame, by mere eruption and expansion almost equals the force of gunpowder, and is also said when mixed with gunpowder to increase its strength.

Again, let the nature in question be the Transitory Nature of Flame and its momentaneous extinction. For the nature of flame appears to have no fixed consistency here with us, but to be every moment generated and every moment extinguished; for it is clear that in flames which continue and last, the continuance we see is not of the same individual flame, but is caused by a succession of new flame regularly generated; nor does the flame remain numerically identical; as is easily seen from this, that if the food or fuel of flame be taken away, the flame instantly goes out. With reference to this nature the roads branch into two, thus. The momentaneous nature proceeds either from a cessation of the cause which at first produced the flame, as in light, sound, and the motion called "violent;" or from this, that the flame, though able by its own nature to remain with us,
[context] suffers violence and is destroyed by the contrary natures that surround it.

This also happens gently in leaves that are somewhat more resistant, as the aqueous part erupts before the oily part catches flame. But this is seen most clearly in Argentum vivum, which is not inappropriately called Aqua mineralis. For this, without combustion, by eruption and simple expansion, almost equals the power of Pulvis Pyrius; it is even said that when mixed with gunpowder, it multiplies its power.

Similarly, let the Natura Inquisita be the transitory nature of flame and its momentary extinction. For the nature of flame does not seem to be fixed and stable here among us, but rather is generated as if at every single moment and immediately extinguished. For it is manifest that in flames which continue and endure here, that duration is not of the same flame as an Individuum, but happens through a succession of new flame generated in order, and by no means does the flame remain the same in number. Bacon analyzes the physics of combustion, noting that "aqueous" substances in materials cause cracking before flames ignite, and that mercury expands with power similar to gunpowder. He further examines the nature of flame, concluding that a persistent flame is not a single, continuous entity but a succession of sparks, and introduces a binary investigation into why flame is fleeting.

[context] 38. I now come to inquire into the second way of condensing the spirits, namely by cold.
For condensation is the proper work of cold; and it is done without any malignity, or unfriendly quality. The operation, therefore, is safer than by opiates, though somewhat less powerful, if used only at intervals, as opiates are. But then since it may be used in moderation familiarly and as a part of daily diet, it has much more power than opiates to prolong life.
[margin] 39.
Refrigeration of the spirits takes place in three ways; by respiration, by vapours, or by aliments. Of these the first is the best, but mostly out of our power; the second likewise is strong, and yet within our reach; the third is weak and circuitous.

2. Those storms attended with cloud and fog, called "belluae," which rise up like pillars, are very violent and dangerous at sea.
3. The greater typhoons, which extend over some considerable space and carry things up into the air along with them, seldom occur; but the lesser and as it were playful eddies and whirlwinds are common.
4. All storms, typhoons, and greater whirlwinds, have a manifest motion of precipitation or vibration downwards, more than the other winds. And hence they appear to rush like torrents, and to flow down as in channels, and to be then repelled by the earth.
5. It sometimes happens that in meadows haycocks are carried up into the air, and then spread abroad like a cover over the field. Again, bundles of pea-straw, sheafs of corn, and linen hung out to dry, are lifted as high as the tops of trees or above the tops of houses by whirlwinds; and all this is done without any great force or violence of wind.
6. Sometimes these very slight and partial whirlwinds take place even on a clear day; so that a person riding may see dust or straws caught up
[context] and whirled round near him without feeling much wind.

[context] In that world every one dwells at a distance from the central region where the Christians are, according to his
confession of the Lord and the one God; for that confession conjoins minds with heaven, and makes the distance from the east, above which is the Lord.
829. Since religion dwells in what is highest in man, and as his lower things have life and light from the highest, and because Mohammed is associated with religion in the minds of Mohammedans, some Mohammed is always placed within their sight; and that they may turn their faces toward the east, over which is the Lord, he is placed beneath the Christian centre. This is not the Mohammed who wrote the Koran, but another who fills his office; nor is there always the same person, but he is changed. He who formerly filled this place was one from Saxony, who having been taken prisoner by the Algerines, became a Mohammedan. This person, because he had also been a Christian, was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, and to say that He was not Joseph's son, but the Son of God Himself. Other Mohammeds afterward succeeded this one. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his station, a fire appears as of a torch to distinguish him; but that fire is not visible to any but Mohammedans.
830. Mohammed who wrote the Koran is not seen at the present day. I was told that at first he presided over them, but that because he wished to rule as God over all things of their religion, he was ejected from his seat, which he had under the Papists, and sent down to the right side near the south. A certain society of Mohammedans was once incited by some malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God. To quiet the disturbance, Mohammed was brought up from the earth below and shown to them; and I also saw him at that time. He appeared like corporeal spirits, who have no inward perception; his face inclined to black. And I heard him utter these words: "I am your Mohammed;" and presently he seemed to sink down.
831. Mohammedans are hostile to Christians chiefly on account of the belief in three Divine Persons, and the consequent worship of three Gods, so many Creators; and to the Roman Catholics, still further, on account of their kneeling before images. Therefore they call these latter idolaters, and the others fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, also that they say one and mutter three; hence that they part omnipotence, and from and of the one omnipotence make three; and that thus they are like fauns with three horns, one for each God, and at the same time three for one; and that so they pray, sing, and preach.
832. Mohammedans, like all nations who acknowledge one God, and who love justice, and do good from religion, have their own heaven, but it is outside of the Christian. The Mohammedan heaven, however, is divided into two. In the lower they live honorably, with more than one wife; but none are raised from this into the higher heaven except those who give up their concubines, and acknowledge the Lord our Saviour, and at the same time His dominion over heaven and hell. I have heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that the Lord rules over the heavens and hells because He is the Son of God the Father. It is through this belief with them, that it is given them by the Lord to ascend into the higher heaven.
833. That the Mohammedan religion is received by more kingdoms than the Christian, may be a stumbling-block to those who think about the Divine Providence, and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except those who are born Christians. But the Mohammedan religion is not a stumbling-block to those who believe that all things are of the Divine Providence; they ask in what this is, and they also find out; it is in this, that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as a very great prophet, the wisest of all, and also as Son of God. But as they have made the Koran the only book of their religion, and consequently Mohammed who wrote it has held his seat in their thoughts, and they follow him with some worship, they therefore think but little about our Lord. That it may be fully known that that religion was raised up from the Lord's Divine Providence, to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it shall be told in some order. First, then, of the origin of idolatries. Previous to that religion, idolatrous worship
[context] was spread through very many kingdoms of the world.

829. Quoniam Religio in ſupremis apud hominem reſidet, & ex ſupremis vivunt & lucent inferiora ejus, & quia Mahumedes verſatur in animis illorum una cum Religione, ideo ſemper aliquis Mahumedes in conſpectu illorum ponitur, ac ut vertant facies ſuas ad Orientem, ſuper quo eſt Dominus, ponitur ille infra Meditullium Chriſtianum: non eſt ipſe Mahumedes, qui Alcoranum conſcripſit, ſed alius qui munere ejus fungitur; nec eſt idem ſemper, ſed mutatur: quondam fuit unus ex Saxonia, qui captus ab Algirienſibus factus eſt Mahumedanus, is quia Chriſtianus etiam fuerat, aliquoties actus eſt ad loquendum cum illis de Domino, quod non fuerit Filius Joſephi, ſed Filius Ipſius Dei. Iſti Mahumedi ſucceſſerunt poſtea alii. In loco ubi repræſentativus ille Mahumedes ſedem habet, apparet ignis ſicut faculæ, ut noſcatur; ſed ille ignis non conſpicuus eſt aliis, quam Mahumedanis.

830. Ipſe Mahumedes, qui ſcripſit Alcoranum, non in conſpectum hodie venit; dictum mihi eſt, quod primis temporibus præfuerit illis, ſed quia voluit dominari ſuper omnia Religionis illorum ut Deus, quod e ſede ſua, quam ſub Pontificiis habuit, ejectus ſit, & ad latus dextrum juxta meridiem demiſſus. Quondam aliqua Societas ex Mahumedanis excitata eſt a malitioſis ad agnoſcendum Mahumedem pro Deo, ut ſeditio ſedaretur, ſublatus eſt Mahumedes ab infera terra, & oſtenſus, & tunc quoque mihi viſus eſt: apparuit ſimilis Spiritibus corporeis, quibus non perceptio interior eſt, facie ad nigrum vergente, & audivi illum loquentem hæc verba, *Ego ſum Mahumedes veſter*; & mox quaſi ſubſidens.

831. Mahumedani infeſti ſunt Chriſtianis primario propter fidem trium Perſonarum Divinarum, & inde cultum trium Deorum, totidem Creatorum, ac Chatolico-Romanis inſuper propter genuflexiones coram ſimulachris, & inde hos vocant Idololatras, & illos fanaticos, dicentes quod faciant Deum Tricipitem, & quod dicant unum ac muſſitent tres, proinde quod ſcindant Omnipotentiam, & ex una & unius faciant tres; & quod ita ſint ſicut Fauni cum tribus cornibus, uno pro quovis Deo, & inſimul tres pro uno, & quod ſic orent, ſic pſallant, & ſic e ſuggeſtibus ſonent.

832. Eſt Mahumedanis, ſicut omnibus Gentibus quæ agnoſcunt Deum unum, ac amant juſtum, & faciunt bonum ex Religione, ſuum Cælum, ſed extra Chriſtianum: aſt Cælum Mahumedanum in duos eſt diſtinctum, in Inferiori vivunt honeſte cum pluribus uxoribus, ſed inde non alii in Cælum ſuperius elevantur, quam qui abdicant pellices, & agnoſcunt Dominum Salvatorem noſtrum, & ſimul Ipſius Dominium ſuper Cælum & Infernum. Audivi quod illis impoſſibile ſit cogitare Deum Patrem & Dominum noſtrum eſſe unum, ſed quod illis poſſibile ſit credere, quod dominetur ſuper Cælos & Inferna, quia Filius Dei Patris eſt: hæc Fides apud illos eſt, per quam aſcenſus in ſuperius Cælum illis a Domino datur.

833. Quod Religio Mahumedana recepta ſit a pluribus Regnis, quam Religio Chriſtiana, poteſt ſcandalo eſſe illis, qui de Divina Providentia cogitant, & ſimul credunt, quod non aliquis ſalvari poſſit, quam qui Chriſtianus natus eſt: at Religio Mahumedana non eſt ſcandalum illis, qui credunt quod omnia ſint Divinæ Providentiæ; hi inquirunt, in quo eſt, & quoque inveniunt. Eſt in hoc, quod Mahumedana Religio agnoſcat Dominum pro Maximo Propheta, Sapientiſſimo omnium, & quoque pro Filio Dei; at quia modo Alcoranum Librum religionis ſuæ fecerunt, & inde Mahumedes, qui illum conſcripſit, cogitationibus illorum inſedit, & aliquo cultu illum proſequuntur, ideo parum de Domino noſtro cogitant. Ut plene ſciatur, quod illa Religio ex Divina Domini Providentia exſuſcitata ſit, ad delendum Idololatrias plurium Gentium, in aliquo ordine dicetur, ſed primum de origine Idololatriarum. 829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a human being, and his lower parts live and shine from these highest parts, and because Mohammed resides in their minds along with their religion, some Mohammed is always placed in their sight. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, upon which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not the Mohammed himself who wrote the Alcoran, but another who performs his duty; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony, who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mohammedan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, saying that He was not the Son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Later, others succeeded this Mohammed. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like a torch so that he may be recognized; but that fire is visible to no one except the Mohammedans.

I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and immediately he seemed to sink down.

[context] The reason why every
coming of the Lord is also signified, is, because by Joseph the Lord is represented as to the Divine Spiritual principle, n. 4669, 4708, 4710; wherefore when it is said, that Joseph should go and see the peace of his brethren, His coming is signified. It is said, every coming, when truth from the Word flows into the thought.
4713. "And the peace of the flock."—That hereby is signified how the case was with those who learnt, or the church, appears (1.) from the signification of peace, as denoting how the case was, see above, n. 4712; and (2.) from the signification of flock, as denoting those who learn: for the shepherd, or he who feeds, is one who teaches and leads to the good of charity; and the flock is he who learns and is led, see n. 343, thus it is the church likewise.
4714. "And bring me word again."—That hereby is signified knowledge, appears from the signification of bringing word again, as denoting to relate how the case was, thus denoting knowledge.
4715. "And he sent him from the valley of Hebron."—That hereby is signified from the Divine Natural and Sensual principle, appears (1.) from the signification of being sent, as denoting to proceed and teach, see above, n. 4710; (2.) from the signification of valley, as denoting those things which are beneath, see n. 1723, 3417; and (3.) from the signification of Hebron, as denoting the Lord's church as to good, see n. 2909. Thus by the above words is signified that he taught those things of the church which are inferior, and this because they did not comprehend superior things; for he who teaches faith and not charity, cannot possibly perceive the superior or interior things of the church, since he has not any thing which guides and dictates whether this be of faith, or true; but if he teaches charity, he then has good, which is to him a dictate, and guides him, for all truth is from and treats of good, or, what is the same thing, the all of faith is from and treats of charity; every one may know from mere natural light, that the all of doctrine has respect to life. That by the above words is signified from the Divine Natural and Sensual principle, is a superior sense; for the inferior things of the church are said to be from the Lord's Divine Natural and Sensual principle; not that these things are inferior in the Lord, for in Him and in His Divine Human principle all is infinite, inasmuch as He is Jehovah as to each essence, n. 2156, 2329, 2921, 3023, but because it is so with man. For they who are sensual men, have a sensual apprehension of those things which are in and from the Lord, and they who are natural have a natural apprehension; the above form of expression is used, owing to the quality of those who receive the Word. But they who are celestial men, and thence truly rational, have a perception of interior things; and it is said of them, that they are taught from the Lord's Divine Rational principle; this is the superior sense, as was said, which is signified by the above words. That a valley denotes the inferior things of the church, may appear from other passages in the Word, as in Isaiah, "The prophecy of the valley of vision. What aileth thee here, that thou hast wholly gone up to the tops of the houses? . . . A day of tumult, and of treading under foot, and of perplexity by the Lord Jehovah Zebaoth, in the valley of vision" xxii. 1, 5; the valley of vision denotes phantasies concerning spiritual things arising from sensual principles, thus from lower things. Again, in the same prophet, "The choice of thy valleys have been filled with chariots, and horsemen have set themselves in array at the gate," xxii. 7; the choice of valleys denotes goods and truths in the natural or external man. Again, "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of Jehovah, make plain in the desert a highway for our God; every valley shall be exalted," xl. 3, 4; where valley denotes the lowly. So in Jeremiah,

4713. Et pacem gregis, quod significet quomodo cum discentibus seu Ecclesia, constat ex significatione pacis, quod sit quomodo se haberet, de qua mox supra n: 4712 ; & ex significatione gregis, quod sint illi qui discunt, pastor enim seu pascens est qui docet & ducit ad bonum charitatis, & grex qui discit & ducitur, de qua n: 343, ita quoque Ecclesia.

3222. Moreover the different kinds of love and their affections are represented by flames, and this with inexpressible variation; but truths are represented by lights, and by innumerable modifications of light; hence it may appear from what ground it is, that by flames in the Word are signified the good things appertaining to love, and by lights the truths appertaining to faith.
3223. There are two lights whereby man is illuminated, the light of the world and the light of heaven; the light of the world is from the sun, the light of heaven is from the Lord; the light of the world is for the natural or external man, thus for those things which are in him; such things although they do not appear to appertain to that light, still do appertain to it, for nothing can be comprehended or conceived by the natural man, except by such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus except they have somewhat of form from the light and shade therein. All ideas of time and of space, which are of so much account in the natural man that he cannot think without them, appertain also to the light of the world. But the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man; the interior mind of man, where are his intellectual ideas which are called immaterial, is in this light; man is ignorant of this, although he calls his intellect sight, and ascribes light to it; the reason is, because so long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he has only a perception of such things as appertain to the light of the world, but not of such things as appertain to the light of heaven; the light of heaven is from the Lord alone, and the universal heaven is in that light. This light, viz., of heaven, is immensely more perfect than the light of the world; the things which in the light of the world make one ray, in the light of heaven make myriads; in the light of heaven is intelligence and wisdom. This is the light which flows into the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive sensually the objects of things; unless this light flowed in, man could not have any perception, for the things appertaining to the light of the world derive hence their life. Between those lights, or between those things which are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is given a correspondence, when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual man, that is, when the former is subservient to the latter; and in this case, the things which exist in the light of the world, are representative of such things as exist in the light of heaven.

3222. Moreover, loves and their affections are represented by flames, and this with inexpressible variation; but truths are represented by lights, and by innumerable modifications of light. From this it can be evident why, in the Word, flames signify the goods of love, and lights signify the truths of faith.

3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are within him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to belong to that light, still exist, for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form through light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which make up so much of the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he has perception only of such things as are of the light of the world, and not of such as are of the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the universal heaven is in that light. This light, namely the light of heaven, is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. The things that form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world, which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception at all, for life from that source is within the things that are of the light of the world. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual, that is, when the former serves the latter; and the things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of such things as are in the light of heaven.

3224. It is remarkable that man does not yet know that his intellectual mind is in a certain light which is entirely different from the light of the world. But such is the condition that, to those who are in the light of the world, the light of heaven is as it were darkness, and to those who are in the light of heaven, the light of the world is as it were darkness. This comes principally from loves, which are the heats of light. Those who are in the loves of self and of the world, and thus in the heat of the light of the world alone, are affected only by evils and falsities, and these are what extinguish the truths that are of the light of heaven. 3222. *In addition, love and their affections are represented by flames, and this variation is inexpressible; Truths, however, are represented by lights, and by innumerable modifications of light; from this it can be seen why flames signify good things which are of love, and lights signify truths which are of faith.*

3223. *There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven; the light of the world comes from the sun, the light of heaven comes from the Lord; the light of the world is for the natural or external man, so for those things which are in him; things which are there, although they do not appear to be of that light, are nevertheless present, for nothing can be taken from the natural man except by those things which exist and appear in the world of the sun, and thus, unless by that light and its shadow, any form is possessed; all ideas of time and ideas of space, which in the natural man only enable him to think, even the light of the world is: but the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man; the inner mind of man, where his intellectual ideas, which are called immaterial, are, is in that light; this man does not know, although he calls his understanding vision, and attributes light to it; the reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily ways, he has perception of such things which are of the light of the world, but not of those which are of the light of heaven; the light of heaven comes from the Lord, the whole heaven is in that light. This light of heaven is infinitely more perfect than the light of the world; what in the light of the world make one ray, in the light of heaven make myriads; in the light of heaven there is understanding and wisdom; this light influences the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and makes him perceive things sensibly; without this light, no perception would exist in man, for life is in those things which are of the light of the world. Between these lights, or between those which are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is correspondence, when the external or natural man unites with the internal or spiritual man, that is, when that one serves this; and what then exists in the light of the world are representative of those which are in the light of heaven.*

3224. *It is wonderful that man does not yet know that his intellectual mind is in a certain light, which is altogether different from the light of the world; but such is the condition that those who are in the light of the world, to them the light of heaven is like darkness, and those who are in the light of heaven, to them the light of the world is like darkness; this comes primarily from loves, which are the heats of light; those who are in love of self and love of the world are affected only by the heat of the light of the world, and these are those which extinguish truths, which are of the light of heaven; those, however, who are in love to the Lord and love for the neighbor*

3222. APPARATUS.
Take some tartarisated Tartar, well prepar'd according to Process 75, dried, and reduc'd to a fine Powder, put it into a tall Bolthead, and pour upon it as much of the purest Alcohol of Wine as will cover it to the height of four inches. With a Paper only stop the Mouth of the Glass, place it in our wooden Furnace, and with a very gentle Fire make the Alcohol boil for the space of a night and a day; and then the Liquor that swims at top will be of a golden Colour, and have an aromatic Smell, and a penetrating warm Taste. If you repeat this in the same manner with fresh Alcohol, there will at last be a white Salt left at the bottom. Let the Tinctures then be inspissated with a moderate Heat, till there is but one tenth part remaining.
USE.
This Operation serves to discover to us that part of this Salt, that may be dissolv'd by Alcohol. The Tincture thus prepar'd is aromatic, heating, cleanses Ulcers, and consolidates Wounds. The remaining Salt too, being purer, and more simple than it was before, teaches us, that by extracting a Tincture from them by Alcohol, even Salts themselves may be render'd whiter.
PROCESS LXXVIII.
A Solution of regenerated Tartar by Alcohol.
APPARATUS.
Upon very dry regenerated Tartar, prepar'd as nicely as possible without destroying its Vertues, and dispos'd in a tall Bolthead, pour six times its weight of the choicest Alcohol, and boil them very cautiously with a gentle Fire in our wooden Furnace. By this means they will become united together into one equable Compound, and there will be some Faeces deposited at the bottom. Let the Vessel stand quiet till the Liquor is well settled, and then gently pour off the clear Tincture from the Faeces, and if there is then any thing saline still remaining, it may be dissolv'd in the same manner with fresh Alcohol. Let these Liquors be put together, and with a very gentle Fire be inspissated to one half, and you will then have a Tincture of this Salt.
USE.
In this Operation you have a vegetable Alcali, an oily vegetable Acid, and an oily vegetable Spirit compounded together. Hence you possess here the most active Principles of Vegetables, freed from their inert Earth, and at the same time not dangerous on account of their Acrimony. This Composition seems to be the Elixir parvum Sapientum, which the antient Chemists so much recommended for preserving and restoring of Health. And certainly it resolves almost all Obstructions, insinuates itself through all the Vessels of the Body, and by a gentle Stimulus makes the animal powers to throw off the morbific Matter by Sweat. In the Chemical Art it proves a most excellent Menstruum, resolving Bodies into their minutest active parts, and thus disposing them to penetrate, with their full seminal Power, into the inmost parts of the Body, and there to overcome the most stubborn resistance. In external Disorders too, as Ulcers, Wounds, and Tumors it is not used with less success. Nor is this valuable Medicine so costly, that the Poor may not share in it, for the regenerated Tartar may be readily prepar'd, by mixing Pot-ashes with fifteen times their quantity of the sharpest Vinegar, and then filtering and inspissating, and then it will cost but little Money or Labour, and yet will be very fit for use. This was known to the ancient Romans. Plin. XXIII. in Proemio. The Ashes of Vine-twigs sprinkled with Vinegar are drank for disorders of the Spleen.
PROCESS LXXIX.
Dr. Harvey's Tincture of Salt of Tartar.
APPARATUS.
Take the very black alcaline Salt, that remains in the Retort, after the volatile part has been forc'd out by the strongest Sand Heat in the Distillation of Tartar, according to Process 55. Upon this, briskly reduc'd to Powder in a hot iron Mortar, and with a hot Pestil, and then put into a tall Bolthead, I pour as much of the best common Spirit of Wine as will cover it to the height of four inches. I then place the Vessel in our wooden Furnace, and with a gentle Fire boil the Mixture for the space of twenty Hours. By this means I have a black thin Liquor, of a bitter, aromatic, lixivious Taste, which I pour off clear, and keep in a close Vessel where it will continue good for a long time. This is Dr. Harvey's Tincture of Salt of Tartar.
USE.
Common Spirit of Wine, consisting of Water, an Acid, and Alcohol united together, by being boil'd with this Alcali of Tartar which still continues oily, makes a Lixivium that is mild and safe, as it is here render'd less acrid by the Acid, the Oil, and the Alcohol, whence arises a kind Medicine, and Menstruum, of considerable Vertues. This being chemically boil'd, and digested with Vegetables is very efficacious in dissolving them. In Surgery it is an excellent remedy for cleansing, deterging, drying, and consolidating moist, purulent, putrid, sanious, virulent Ulcers, as well fistulous, as sinuous: In fungous Excrescences too it is used to eat them down with good success, especially if it is mixed according to art, with a small quantity of Oil. Taken internally likewise, it has admirable effects, in those Diseases, where an acid, rough, watery, mucous, pituitous or earthy Matter abounds, as also in Coagulations, provided
[context] there is no putrid dissolution of the Humours.

### PROCESS LXXVII.
**Tincture of Tartarized Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**ake Tartarized Tartar, duly prepared according to Process 75, and dried, then ground into a fine powder. Pour over it, in a tall chemical vial, the purest Alcohol of wine to a depth of four inches. Then, with the vial closed only with paper, let them boil together, as gently as possible, in our wooden furnace for the space of twenty-four hours. The Alcohol will be of a golden color, floating on top, with an aromatic odor and a penetrating, warm taste. If this is repeated with fresh Alcohol in the same manner, a white salt will eventually be left at the bottom. The tinctures are thickened by a gentle fire, so that a tenth part remains, concentrated at the bottom.

#### USES.
**I**t serves to demonstrate the part in that Salt which is dissolved by the Alcohol. The Tincture itself, when prepared, is aromatic and warming, and consolidates ulcers and wounds. The remaining salt, being simpler than before, teaches that salts themselves can be whitened, once the tincture has been drawn out by the aid of Alcohol.

### PROCESS LXXVIII.
**Dissolution of Regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**ake Regenerated Tartar, prepared as neatly as possible beforehand, and, as safely as can be done, pour six times its amount of the purest Alcohol into a tall, glass chemical vial. Boil it over a gentle fire in our wooden furnace, as prudently as possible. They will combine with each other, and these will become one uniformly composed substance, with the dregs deposited at the bottom. After they have then settled accurately through rest, let the supernatant and pure liquor flow off by a careful tilting of the vessel. If any saline matter not yet dissolved remains, it can be dissolved by the application of fresh Alcohol with the same caution, and separated from the dregs. Then indeed, let the prepared liquors be thickened by distilling over a very gentle fire until they are reduced to half, and the Tincture of this Salt will be obtained.

#### USES.
**Y**ou see in this experiment united into one: alkali, oily acid, and the oil of spirits of vegetables. Hence, the most active principles of plants are freed from inert earth; yet at the same time they are sufficiently safe, and their acrimony is no longer dangerous. These, indeed, when thus united, seem to constitute even the small Elixir of the Sages, which the masters of the ancient Art recommended for preserving and restoring health. It heals almost all obstructions, penetrates through the vessels,
and excites life with an agreeable stimulus: it heals through perspiration. In chemical operations, it also provides a most effective solvent, by which substances are reduced to their smallest parts, with their active, seminal virtue unimpaired, so that they may be admitted into the inner chambers of the body to check and tame whatever is rebellious. Nor is this remedy less praised for the beauty of the effects it produces on external bodily ailments, wounds, ulcers, and tumors. Yet this remedy, being so wholesome, should not be denied to the poor out of ambition: for it can be prepared immediately by mixing potash with fifteen parts of the sharpest Vinegar, filtering, and thickening it. Thus, it can be prepared and used without the expense of labor and cost. Known to the ancients in Rome. Pliny, Book XXIII, in the Preface: "The ash of vine-shoots, sprinkled with vinegar, is drunk for ailments of the spleen."

### PROCESS LXXIX.
**Harvey’s Tincture of Salt of Tartar.**

To this, quickly pounded into a powder in a hot iron mortar by a hot pestle, and placed into a tall glass vial, I pour the best common spirits of wine, such that they stand four fingers above it. I boil it over a gentle fire in this tall vial, in our wooden furnace, for twenty hours. A black, thin liquor will be obtained, with a bitter, aromatic, and lixivial taste. Let this be poured off pure. Thus, it may be kept safely in a closed vessel for its due uses, under its own title.

It is also used to consume growths that arise from excessive flesh, especially if it is mixed with a little oil according to art. ### PROCESSUS LXXVII.
**Tincture of Tartar that has been Tarterized.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**artar that has been Tarterized, properly prepared, as in Processus 75, and a fico, then pour into a narrow flask, and fill it with pure wine alcohol to four fingers above. Then, in a single flask covered with paper, let it gently boil in our wooden furnace, during the night. It will result in alcohol of a golden color, aromatic, penetrating, and warm. If this is repeated with new alcohol in the same way. Finally, a white residue will remain at the bottom. The tinctures are thickened with a gentle fire, so that one tenth remains in the bottom.

#### U S U S.
**S**erves to demonstrate the part in that salt which is dissolved by alcohol. The prepared tincture, aromatic, warming, heals wounds and sores. The remaining salt, simpler than before, shows that the pure salts can be whitened, by the aid of the tinctured alcohol.

### PROCESSUS LXXVIII.
**Dissolution of Regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**artar that has been regenerated, as clean as possible, previously, and as much as possible, pour into a high, glass flask, five times the amount of pure alcohol, and cook gently in our wooden furnace, as carefully as possible. They will combine with each other, forming a single, evenly composed substance, and the residue will settle at the bottom. After they have rested in quiet, with a careful inclination of the vessel, the upper liquid, pure and clear, will flow out. If any salt still remains undissolved, it can be dissolved with fresh alcohol, using the same care, and separated by filtration. Then, the prepared liquids, with a very gentle fire, are distilled to half their volume, and the tincture of this salt is obtained.

#### U S U S.
**Y**ou recognize this in an experiment, gathered into one, alkali, oleous acid, spirit of oils, and vegetable matter. From this, the most active principles of plants, freed from inert earth; yet still sufficiently safe, and not dangerously sharp. These, thus gathered, seem to constitute even a small Elixir of the Wise, which the masters of the old Art recommended for the preservation and restoration of health. It heals almost all obstacles, penetrates through vessels, and with a pleasant stimulus, incites life, causing diaphoresis. In Chemistry, it also provides the most effective solvent, by which things are reduced to the smallest, active, pure female virtue, so that they may be admitted into the inner parts of the body, to overcome and conquer rebellious conditions. It is also praised for the effects it produces on external bodily ailments, wounds, sores, tumors. It is not less praised as a remedy for the poor, so beneficial: it can be made immediately, by mixing clavellated ashes with fifteen times the strongest vinegar, filtering, and thickening: thus, it can be made and used without labor or expense. Known in ancient Rome. Pliny, XXIII, in Procemio. Ashes of grain, mixed with vinegar, are drunk for the ailments of the spleen.

### PROCESSUS LXXIX.
**Tincture of Harvey's Salt.**

#### APPARATUS.
**I** take the alkaline salt, very black, which remains in the glass retort after all volatile matter from the tartar has been driven off by distillation, as in (Proc. 55). To this, I grind it in a hot iron mortar with a hot pestle, quickly into powder, and pour it into a high glass flask, and pour over it the best, common wine spirit, so that it rises to four fingers. I cook it gently in this high flask, in our wooden furnace, for twenty hours. A black, thin liquid, with a bitter, aromatic, and extractive taste, is obtained. This liquid is pure. Thus, it can be safely kept in a closed vessel for its proper use.

#### U S U S.
**W**ine spirit, water, acid, and alcohol, when united, boiling with tartar alkali, yet still oleous, produces a milder, safer extract: due to the tempered acid, oil, and alcohol, the alkali; from which the species of medicine and menstruum, not ignoble, is born. This, when cooked or digested with vegetables, beautifully dissolves simples, and is of great value. In Surgery, it is the noblest remedy for purging, cleansing, drying, and healing, moist, putrid, foul, and virulent sores, ulcers, and canker, both fistulous and sinuous, and those that are tunnel-like; and for consuming those that luxuriously grow in excess; especially if mixed with a little oil from the art. It also excellently serves internally for all diseases in which acid, harsh, watery, mucous, phlegmatic, earthy, and coagulated matter abound.

### PROCESS LXXVII.
**Tincture of Tartarized Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
**Tartarized Tartar**, properly prepared according to Process 75, and dry, then pour into a high chemical phial, with four fingers' breadth of the purest wine alcohol superfluous. Then, with the phial alone closed with paper, let them boil together, as gently as possible, in our wooden furnace, for the space of a night. There will be an alcohol of a golden color floating on top, with an aromatic odor, a penetrating taste, and warm. If this is repeated with new alcohol in the same way. Finally, a white salt will remain at the bottom. Let the tinctures be thickened with a gentle fire, so that a tenth part remains collected at the bottom.

#### USE.
**It serves to demonstrate the part in that Salt which is dissolved by the Alcohol.** The tincture itself, prepared and aromatic, heating, consolidating ulcers and wounds. The remaining salt, simpler than before, teaches that the salts themselves can be whitened, with the help of the tincture of alcohol.

### PROCESS LXXVIII.
**Dissolution of regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
**Regenerated Tartar**, which has been prepared as cleanly as possible beforehand, and as much as possible safely, pour into a high, chemical, glass phial, six times the amount of the purest alcohol, and boil with a gentle fire in our wooden furnace, as prudently as possible. They will combine with each other, and one certain composition will be made from these, with the dregs deposited at the bottom. After they have then subsided accurately through quiet, let the floating, pure liquid flow out with the vessel inclined prudently. If any salt not yet dissolved remains, it can be dissolved by the application of fresh alcohol with the same caution, and separated by settling. Then, the prepared liquids, by distilling with a very gentle fire, will be forced to half, and the Tincture of this Salt will be had.

#### USE.
**You discern this in the experiment gathered into one, the alkali, the oily acid, the oily spirits, and the vegetable.** Hence, the most active principles of plants, freed from inert earth; yet at the same time sufficiently safe, and not more dangerous than the sharpness. These, indeed, gathered in this way, seem to constitute also the small Elixir of the Wise, which the masters of the ancient Art commended for preserving and restoring health. It heals almost all obstacles, it penetrates through the vessels, it incites life with a lovable stimulus: so that it heals through diaphoresis. In Chemicals also, it provides a most effective solvent, by which they are reduced to the smallest, active, and unblemished seminal virtue, so that they can thus be admitted into the inner chambers of the body, to suppress and tame every rebellion. Nor is it less praised for the beauty of the effects which it provides for the external evils of the body, wounds, ulcers, tumors. Nor, however, is this remedy so ambitious that it is denied to the poor, so healthy: for it can be prepared immediately, by mixing the clavellated ashes with fifteen times the sharpest vinegar, by straining, and thickening: so that it can be prepared and used without labor and expense, and usurped. Known to the ancients in Rome. Pliny, Book 23, in the Proem. Ash of grain sprinkled with vinegar is drunk for the ailments of the spleen.

### PROCESS LXXIX.
**Harvey's Tincture of Salt of Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
**I take the alkaline salt, very black, which remained in the glass retort after all volatile matter was expelled by distillation from the Tartar at a high fire, according to (Proc. 55).** To this, in a hot iron mortar, quickly ground into powder by a hot pestle, and put into a high glass phial, I pour the best, common spirits of wine, so that they float to four fingers. I boil with a gentle fire in this high phial, in our wooden furnace, for twenty hours. There will be a black, thin liquid, with a bitter, aromatic, and lye-like taste. Which is poured out pure. Thus, the vessel closed can be safely kept for its due uses.

[context] Afterward We administer it with the same Preparation, and the same Projection, pouring it upon the Substance of Luna. And yet thence results not a
splendid bright Colour, but dull and livid, with a mortiferous Citrinity.
But the way of colouring it, which is made by Vitriol, or Copperas, is thus: ℞ of either of them a certain Quantity, and sublime as much thereof, as can be sublimed, until with great expression of Fire it be sublimed. After this again sublime this Sublimate with Fire appropriate to it, that of it part after part may be fixed, until its greater part is fixed. But afterward, it must be warily calcined, that a greater Fire may be administred for its Perfection. This being done, it is dissolved into a most Red Water, that hath not its Peer. Then so operate, as you may give it Ingress into the Lunar Body. These Processes are sufficiently demonstrated to you, if you be a true Searcher of the perfect Work, as We have described it. For We, seeing things of this kind profoundly and amicably to adhere to Luna, have considered (and it is certain) that these are from its own Radix; and thence it is, that Luna is altered by them. These Medicines, which We have here inferred, are all of the first Order. Yet there may be manifold other Methods of these Medicines, salving the Essence of Pigmental Things, in the Variety of Methods. [For the Medicine of Argentvive is not in this first Order, seeing it is not a Medicine altering Luna with one only Difference, but altogether in total Compleatment.] Others have invented many Medicines, yet one of these two necessarily happens, viz. either they are constrained to create the Medicine of the same Things, or of Things having the same Nature; or else they compound a Medicine, which with its Alteration is equivalent to that, which it is not, and which neither confers to the Clean, nor to the Parts of the Clean, until the Mover, in the sublime Mobile of Nature, rests uncorrupt.

[context] Therefore, let him be careful, that he err not in exposing Saturn, after its first Pulverization to too great a Fire, and so reduce the Calx into Body, before it is perfected. For he needs
Temperance of Fire, and that leisurely augmented by degrees, with Caution, until it be confirmed in its Calx; proving not so easily reducible, that a greater Fire may be administred to it, for compleatly perfecting its Calx. Likewise, he must be careful, that he err not in Jupiter, by reason of its difficult Reduction; so, that when he intends to reduce its Calx, he find it not reduced, but in its former condition, or turned into Glass; and thence he conclude its Reduction impossible. For We say, if a great Fire be not administred, in the Reduction of Tin, it reduceth not; and if a great Fire be administred, it doth not necessarily happen, that it shall be reduced; but 'tis possible it may be converted to Glass. And that is, because Jupiter, in the profundity of its Nature, hath the fugitive Substance of Argentvive included: which, if kept long in Fire, flies away, and leaves the Body deprived of Humidity; so that it is found more apt for Vitrification, than to be converted to the Fusion of a Metallick Body. For every Thing deprived of its proper Humidity, gives no other than a Vitrificatory Fusion. Whence it necessarily follows, that the Artist must hasten to reduce it swiftly, with the speedy force of a violent Fire: for otherwise it is not reduced. Therefore let him practice therein, and he will come to the Knowledg thereof.
The way of Calcination of these two Bodies, which is performed by the Acuity of Salt, is, that Quantity after Quantity of Salt be very often cast upon them in their Fusion, and permixed by much agitation with a Rod of Iron over the Fire, until by mixtion of the Salt they be turned into Ashes. And afterward, by the same way of Perfection, the Calxes of them are perfected, with their Considerations. But in this also there is difference in the Calcination of these two Bodies. For Lead, with the first labours of Calcination, is more easily converted to Powder than Tin; yet the Calx of it is not more easily perfected, than the Calx of Tin. The Cause of this Diversity is, because Saturn hath a more fixed Humidity than Jupiter.

Fire that is being used requires, and through the gradual increase of that, with care, until its base is firmly established, so that it does not easily return to the body, so that a greater fire may be administered to it, for the perfection of its base. Similarly, it should not happen that it goes astray in Jupiter, because of the difficulty of its reduction, so that if, when it is placed in the reduction of its base, it happens that it does not reduce it, but finds it either in the prior disposition or reduced to the vessel, and estimates its reduction as impossible. For we say that if in the reduction of Jupiter a great fire is not applied, it will not be reduced. But if a great fire is applied, it is not necessary that it be reduced, but it is possible to reduce it to vitrification. And this is because Jupiter has, in the depth of its nature, a living silver fugitive included, a substance. If this is drawn out for a long time in fire, it will flee, and leave behind a body deprived of moisture, so that it is rather suitable for vitrification than for the fusion of metallic body. For every substance deprived of moisture gives no fusion except vitrification. Therefore, it necessarily follows that with the most rapid impetus of fire, it must be reduced quickly. For otherwise it is not reduced. Therefore, it is practiced for this, and it will know.

The second method of calcination of these two bodies, Saturn and Jupiter, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that the quantity of salt is thrown upon the surface of these salts, after the quantity has been most frequently in its own fusion, and is mixed with many agitations through a metal rod, upon fire, until through the mixture of salt they are turned into ash. And then, by the same method of perfection, their lime is completed, with their considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. For lead is more easily converted into powder from the first calcination labor than Jupiter, but it is not more easily completed into lime than Jupiter. This depends upon the cause, because Saturn has more fixed moisture than Jupiter.

[context] Take the stone, whiche is called Esmundus or Asmadus, it is of diuers colours, it putteth out all poyson, and maketh a man to ouercome hys
aduersaries, & geueth Prophesieng, and the interpretation of all dreames, & maketh a man to vnderstande darke questions, harde to be vnderstād or assoyled.
¶ If thou wilt haue good vnder standing of thynges that may be felte, and that thou maye not be made dronked.
Take the stone, whithe is called Amaristus, and it is of purple colour, and the beste is founde in Inde, and it is good agaynst drūkennes, and geueth good vnderstandynge in thynges that maye be vnderstande.
¶ If thou wilt ouercom thy enemyes, and slee debate.
Take the stone, whiche is called Berillus, it is of pale coloure and may be sene through as water, bear it about with thee, and thou shalt ouercome all debate, & shalte dryue a waye thy enemies and it maketh thy enemye meke. It causeth a manne too be well manuered, as Aaron sayethe, it geueth also good vnderstādinge.
¶ If thou wilt foreiudge, or coniecture of thynges to come.
¶ Take the stone, whiche is called Celonites, it is of purple, & diuerse other colours, & it is foūde in the head of the snayle. If any man will beare thys stone vnder hys tunge, he shal foreiudge, and propheci of thinges to come. But notwithstanding, it hath no vertue, but shynynge, Prima cum fuerit accensa, et crescens monoytes in vltima descendente, soo meaneth Aaron, in the boke of vertues of herbes, and stones.
¶ If thou wilt pacifie tempestes and go ouer fluddes.
¶ Take the stone, which is called Corallus, Corall, & some be read and some whyte. And it hath ben proueth that it stemmeth anone bloude, and putteth away the folishnes of hym that beareth it, & geueth wysedom. And this hath ben proued of certayn mē in our tyme. And it is good agaynst tempestes, and perils of fluddes.

¶ If you wish to have a good intellect for the senses: and to not be able to become drunk: Take the stone which is called **Amethyst**: and it is of a purple color: and the best is born in India and it is effective against drunkenness. And it confers good intellect in knowable things.

+
¶ If you wish to overcome enemies and flee litigations. Take the stone which is called **Beryl**: and it is of a pale color, of a light transparent like water: Carry it with you and you will conquer all litigations and you will put enemies to flight: and it will render the enemy mild. It renders one powerful in manners: just as Aaron says. It also gives good intellect in knowable things.

¶ If you wish to divine about future things. Take the stone which is called **Chelonitis**: and it is of a purple and various color: and it is found in the body of a tortoise. If anyone, however, shall have carried this stone under the tongue he will divine and predict future things. Nevertheless it does not have power unless it is shining first when it has been ignited: and growing in the last quarter descending. Thus Aaron wishes concerning the powers of stones and herbs.

+
If you wish to pacify tempests and to cross rivers. Take the stone which is called **Coral** and it is red and some are white. And it is expert testimony that it immediately restrains blood and being carried it drives away stupidity: and proffers wisdom: and this has been tested by some in our time: and it is valid against tempests: and the dangers of rivers.

### CHAP. XXI.

Now we shall recount the fruits from which wines may be made, but first those produced by the ancients, in a twofold difference: for some are for remedies, with which books of physicians are filled, others are for use, and they are of nearly infinite kinds, according to the differences of places and peoples: for that which is given to one is denied to another. First

->*Wine from palms*<-

or a hare's fur, or the dung that holds the hair, or those who have the peristereon herb. A black stone, similar to a bean, is found in the Nile; when this is seen, dogs do not bark. You shall carry a dog’s tongue placed under the thumb in your shoe, or if you carry the dried heart of a dog with you, according to Sextus; or hare’s fur or dung, according to Pliny. Or you shall carry the tail of a young weasel cut off in your foot, or give it a frog in a morsel of food; all these are for avoiding the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs flee the sight of anyone all day who expels a tick from a dog and carries it for a while. Oppian:

> Astonished by sharp terror, will not bark at you
> As you approach, even if they were barking before.

### *That a dog may not be able to run.*

If you smear the wings with oil, for it will be hindered in running; in this way, it will happen.

### *That a hawk may be spirited.*

You shall animate the bird against its prey, so that it attacks large birds; moisten the bait, which it uses at the time of hunting, with wine, or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from its beak into a pigeon chick, then make it fly. Thus:

If you give them twigs of maidenhair fern in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### *Roosters become more combative,*

By giving garlic in their food when they are about to fight; from which most facetiously in ancient comedy they are called eskorodismenoi, that is, garlic-stuffed, used for someone vehement and overly prone to fighting.

### *That a bird may not fly high,*

Pull out the feathers of the tail, which direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### *That a bird may not be able to fly,*

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way, they do not escape in aviaries.

[context] Also the Archeus daily dispenseth so much of the venal Blood to the parts proportionally, as they have need of for their own nourishment.
[margin] 15.
Therefore the Pus or corrupt matter, is venal Blood vitiated in that part wherein the Wound is, and an effect of digestion vitiated in the same place.
Therefore to have vitiated the entireness, continuation or holding together, and digestion of the parts, next, to have converted the venal Blood into corrupt Snotty matter, is reputed the very same thing in the Schools, as to have gone to prevent Catarrhs or Rheums; or thorow the hole of a Cautery, to have extracted from the Head (from whence they originally fetch all Rheums) an excrementous humor, which otherwise had threatned to fall down on a noble part; whether in the mean time, there be an agreement between the Head, and the Wounded part or not; for it is all one, so the Skin be deteined Wounded, whether that excrementous humour be Blood, or be made snotty pus, or liquid Sanies, is all one, so by the thred-bare words of Catarrhe, prevention, derivation, revulsion, and an Issue, the world be circumvented. For I behold a small Infant of a Year old, now breeding Teeth, and to suffer a Fever, froath of the Mouth, and Spittle, without ceasing; And at length that there are wringings of the Bowels, and Stools of Yellow-Green-coloured excrements: At least that Tooth is a part of the Head, wherefore the Flux shall be a Rheum of the Head: But what consent is there of a Tooth about to break forth, or a swollen Gum with a Bowel? Or what power thereof is there of begetting or sending away that Catarrhe out of the Stomack of a little Infant, unto his Head? And from thence into the Ileos? By what right shall a vapour dropped or stilled out of the Stomack, be made Cankered Choler in the Head? Hath perhaps the shop of Choler now wandred from the beginning of Life unto the Head? Could a Cautery (if an Infant were for undergoing it) suck unto it a leeky Flux into it self? And by a few small drops of corrupt matter, recompence or Ballance the leeky Choler of some pounds? Why doth the Stomack of a small Infant frame a Catarrhe by reason of the pain of his Tooth? Why is it sent into a Bowell, and not unto the paining Tooth? Doth not the reader yet see, that a Flux is not a Rheum? But that the Archeus (wheresoever yee will have it) being enraged, is ready in the Bowels, to transchange the nourishable juyce into excrements, which by the Schools are reckoned Choler, Phlegme, &c. If therefore the Flux be not a Rheume, and the Archeus being wroth, can transchange any thing into a troublesom Liquor, if the Gum be but afflicted; shall not he be able, on every side to unload himself by the appointed emunctories? And not to wait for the Skin to be opened by a Caustick? Alass, hath cruel dullness caused the Schools to be cruel towards their mortal kinsfolks?
[margin] 16.
For neither do they consider, that in Women, and those that are somewhat fat or gross, there is in the fleshly membrane, about the ordinary places of a Cautery, a meer grease to the thickness of two fingers at least, for which persons notwithstanding, the more frequent Cauteries (and those the more profitable ones) are perswaded; wherefore also the bottom of the Issue shall scarce be in the middle of the grease:
[margin] 17.
therefore there is not a passage, whereby the evil banished feigned humour of a Rheume, may rush down out of the Brain, or between the Scull, and Skin, thorow the middle of the fat.
But what is that solitary humour, in the next place, which for its offence, being banished from the sending part, descending thorow the Substance of the grease unmixed, doth degenerate into corrupt Pus? If it be an exhalation of vapours out of the Stomack, why shall it not be more frequent to younger and hot Stomacks, than to weak, old, and cold ones? In what sort shall that water that droppeth out of a vapour, put on the form of Snotty matter? How shall it hasten thorow the Brain, Coats and Scull, to find a hole made by a Cautery, that it may flow down thither only, and be purged? Why doth not the vapour fly, first an hundred times into the Air, before it reach to the place appointed it by the alluring Cautery? How shall the Water which climbeth from the Stomack, be now venal Blood, and the mother of corrupt snotty matter? <margin>15.</margin>
Ergò pus, est cruor vitiatus in illa parte qua vulnus est, effectusque vitiatæ ibidem digestionis. Vitiâsse ergo partium integritatem, continuitatem, atque digestionem, cruorem denique in pus convertisse, idipsum est in *Scholis* reputatum, *Catarrhis* obviam ivisse : sive à capite (undè omnes *Catarrhos* originaliter petunt) humorem excrementosum (qui alioquin ad partem nobilem comminatus erat decumbere) per foramen cauterii extraxisse : sive interim capiti, cum parte vulnerata, sit consensus, vel non: perindè enim est, modo cutis faucia detineatur. Sivè humor ille excrementosus, sit cruor, sivè pus fiat, vel sanies, perindè, modò per trita vocabula Catarrhi, præcautionis, derivationis, revulsionis, & fontanellæ, mundo fit circumventum. Contueor enim hornotinum infantulum, jam dentientem, ac pati febrim, spumam oris, atque indefinentem salivam. Ac tandem adesse tormina, & secessus ex viridi flaventibus. Saltem dens ille est capitis pars: quapropter diarrhœa erit Catarrhus capitis. Ast quis est dentis erupturi, vel tumidæ gingivæ consensus cum intestino? quæve potestas ejus gignendi, immittendi Catarrhi, è stomacho infantuli ad caput? atque indè in *Ileon*? quo jure stillatus è stomacho vapor, fiet æruginosa bilis in capite? fortè nè ab vitæ initio jam biles officina migravit ad caput? An cauterium posset (si infans esset tolerando) diarrhœam porraceam in se affugere? paucisque puris guttulis compensare aliquot librarum bilem porraceam? Cur fabricat Infantuli stomachus Catarrhum, propter dentis dolorem? Cur mittitur in Intestino, & non ad dentem dolentem? An nondum cernit lector, diarrhœam non esse Catarrhum? Sed indignatum *Archeum* ubilibet, in Intestino promtum esse, ad transmutandum alimentarium cremorem in excrementa, quæ à *Scholis* putantur bilis, pituita, &c. Si itaque diarrhœa non fit Catarrhus, possitque *Archeus* indigna-

<column-break/>

tus transmutare quilibet in infestum liquorem, si modo gingiva affligatur; An non poterit quaqua versus se exonerare per statuta emunctoria? nec præstolari apertam pellem caustico? Ah crudelis hebetudo, ferocire *Scholas* fecit in mortales sibi agnatos?
<margin>16.</margin>
Neque enim considerant, quod in mulieribus, & obesis, carnosa membrana sit circa ordinaria loca cauterii, mera axungia ad duorum saltem digitorum spissitudinem, quibus tamen personis frequentiora, magisque proficua, persuadentur cauteria. Quare etiam vix in medietate axungiæ fundus fontanellæ erit: 
<margin>17.</margin>
Non est ergò via, qua è cerebro, vel inter cranium, & cutim, ruat malus, *Catarrhi* proscriptus humor fictitius, per medium adipis. Sed quis demum humor ille solitarius, suo qui peccato à parte mittente proscriptus, per axungiæ substantiam, impermistus descendens, in pus degenerat? Si sit exhalatio vaporum è stomacho, cur non erit frequentior junioribus, & calidis stomachis, quam debilibus, senibus & frigidis? Quo pacto aqua ista, è vapore stillatitia, formam puris induet? # C A U T E R I U M.

15.
Therefore, pus is blood corrupted in the very part where the wound is, and it is the effect of a digestion that has been corrupted there. To have corrupted the integrity, continuity, and digestion of the parts, and finally to have converted blood into pus, is what has been esteemed in the *Schools* to be the same as having averted Catarrhs: whether by extracting through the opening of the cautery an excremental humor (which otherwise had threatened to settle upon a noble part) from the head, from whence they all originally seek their *Catarrhs*: or whether or not there be a consensus between the head and the wounded part; for it is the same thing, provided the wounded skin is kept open. Whether that excremental humor be blood, or becomes pus, or sanies, it is the same, provided the world is circumvented through the worn-out terms of Catarrh, precaution, derivation, revulsion, and fontanella. For I observe a year-old infant, now teething, suffering from fever, mouth foam, and ceaseless saliva. And finally, there are gripings and stools of a yellowish-green color. At least that tooth is a part of the head: therefore, diarrhea will be a Catarrh of the head. But what is the consensus of an erupting tooth, or of a swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what is its power of generating, of sending a Catarrh from the infant’s stomach to the head? And thence into the *Ileon*? By what right will a vapor distilled from the stomach become greenish bile in the head? Has the workshop of bile perhaps migrated to the head since the beginning of life? Could a cautery (if the infant were capable of enduring it) drive the porraceous diarrhea into itself? And compensate for several pounds of porraceous bile with a few tiny drops of pus? Why does the infant’s stomach manufacture a Catarrh because of a toothache? Why is it sent into the intestine, and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a Catarrh? But rather that the indignant *Archeus* anywhere, being ready in the intestine to transmute the alimentary chyme into excrements, which are thought by the *Schools* to be bile, phlegm, etc. If, therefore, diarrhea is not a Catarrh, and the indignant *Archeus* can

transmute whatever he likes into a harmful liquid, provided the gum is afflicted, could he not exonerate himself in every direction through established emunctories ? And not wait for the skin to be opened by a caustic? Ah, cruel dullness, has it made the *Schools* behave fiercely toward mortals born of the same stock?
16.
For they do not consider that, in women and obese people, the fleshy membrane around the ordinary sites of the cautery is mere lard to a thickness of at least two fingers, yet it is to these persons that more frequent and more beneficial cauteries are recommended. Wherefore, the base of the *fontanella* will scarcely be in the middle of the fat.
17.
There is therefore no path by which the evil, fictitious humor—proscribed as a *Catarrh*—may rush from the brain, or from between the cranium and the skin, through the middle of the fat. But what, finally, is that solitary humor, which, having been proscribed by its own fault by the part sending it, descending unmixed through the substance of the fat, degenerates into pus? If it were an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why would it not be more frequent in the young, and those with warm stomachs, than in the weak, the old, and the cold? In what way will this water, distilled from vapor, put on the form of pus? How will it hasten through the brain, the meninges, and the cranium to find the opening made by the cautery, so that it may flow out and be purged only by that path? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times before it reaches the place designated by the compliant cautery? How will water climbing from the stomach be blood and the matter of pus? How will blood (the matter of pus, according to *Galen*) be the matter of *Catarrh*? Why must blood be reduced to the series of bad humors, which, not yet contaminated, is dispensed by nature to the wounded place? Why, once a wound is made, will nature cease to disturb the condemned matter through and into its accustomed places? For once the skin is opened at the pleasure of the healer, will it become ignorant of deviations? Or has it perhaps labored only to find an exit somewhere? And having done so, will it henceforth come to the bidding of the one inflicting the wound? Thus these four are false,

Van Helmont argues that the discharge from medical cauteries is not the drainage of harmful humors or "catarrh" from the head, but rather the corruption of healthy blood caused by the artificial wound itself. He criticizes the medical establishment for ignoring anatomical realities, such as the layer of fat that prevents deep drainage, and dismisses the theory of catarrh as a fictitious explanation for vital processes he attributes to the Archeus.

plainly, the greatest part of diseases, coming from Celestial Influence, and from the Astral Impression of the greater and lesser Worlds firmament, admit not of cure with promiscuous Remedies, as by Arcanums of Herbs, Minerals, and Metalls, but by Astronomick Influence, the cure is instituted with such things only as have an Analogy to the greater and lesser World, in which is the true Magnetick force of the Firmament, and a Celestial Impression of resisting diseases, caused by the Firmament of the greater and lesser World, as is apparent in Arsemart, the greater Comphry, Dragonwort, and the greater Wallwort. If supernaturally, the disease or dolour take its beginning from Inchantment or by Magical Impression of Ascendants, the endeavouring the Cure by the three former ways is fruitless and unprofitable; but according to Paracelsus, process must be made Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil by the same means it was inferr'd must again be expell'd. In the aforesaid Simples there is an Influential Attractive, and all according to Divine Ordination, Magically, Astronomically, and Magnetically cure; because in them is Medicine, and in Man the Magnet.
For as the Sun and Stars have power of attracting humidity from Inferiours, so Man (by the Magnetick attractive virtue placed in him, attracts Spirit instead of Nutriment, as a Loadstone draws Iron) and Inferiors have the same power of attracting from Superiors, as we see in time of the Pest; and these
[margin] ... Astral, Venenate, and Spiritual, the fift is such as are inflicted as a Scourge.
[margin] These Astral and Firmamental Infections are known by the ingenious Physician, and Firmamentally cured, for Art hath obtained a Medicine which impowers the Phy[s]itian ... to know and expell Firmamental diseases.
[margin] The Magnet of Man is Magical Cure, in which is a Celestial Impression after Contact of the Herb, the Herb until it be putrefied, attracts Medicine into the Ulcer, and so cures it.

[context] and moreover in this Hydropick Specifick, he joyns it with the Extract of black Hellebore and Colequintida,
that their virtues may be rendred more strong in expelling, and also the doses of precipitate Mercury, for their more commodious exhibiting he appoints to be made up in Pills. Therefore this precipitate Mercury, is by him highly praised and commended, and not without cause, for it powerfully helps in this case. Of like virtue is Mercurius vitae, or Flowers of Butter of Antimony, of which above, if from four granes to twelve thereof, be exhibited for three days together in extract of Hellebore and Colequintida; they happily expell the resolved Salt. But afterward Sweats and Urine must be provoked, with a decoction of Sarsaparilla, Lignum Sanctum, or root of Colts-foot, adding always a little Spirit of Tartar, or other Diaphoreticks and Diureticks, of which above; but especially adding Arcanum of Wormwood, or Carduus Benedictus. But this is to be noted, that the exhibiting of Mercurius vitae three days together, in those of ripe age, is often wont to cause the falling down of the Fundament, which is afterward rarely, or at most very difficultly cured. Yet it is needful in cure of the Dropsie, that such Purgations be adhibited in the beginning, but afterward Diureticks and Hydroticks must succeed. For otherwise, viz. ὕστερον πρότερον, this will happen, the Whey, or Watery humidity will all be devolved to the Reins Urinal Passages, from whence afterward, by reason of aggravation, very often most pertinacious Symptomes are wont to arise. Moreover in preparation of the Extract of Root of black Hellebore, it will be more safe instead of Spirit of Wine, to take Wine it self, with which the Root must only be gently Boiled without noise, and this done with fresh Wine, so long as until all the Essencified force be Extracted from the Root, afterward by evaporating or distilling reduce the Extract to the thickness of Honey. For Spirit of Wine, by reason of its attraction, which it rather acts upon the Sulphur, then the
[context] Mercurial liquor, in which the purging virtue consists, is less profitable, therefore Wine is better.
