to return to their manner of living in society: the oldest man of every family, as has been already said, is its governor; wives serve their husbands, and children their parents, and always the younger serves the elder. Every city is divided into four equal parts, and in the middle of each there is a market-place. What is brought thither, and manufactured by the several families, is carried from thence to houses appointed for that purpose, in which all things of a sort are laid by themselves; and thither every father goes, and takes whatsoever he or his family stand in need of, without either paying for it or leaving anything in exchange. There is no reason for giving a denial to any person, since there is such plenty of everything among them; and there is no danger of a man’s asking for more than he needs; they have no inducements to do this, since they are sure they shall always be supplied:

of citizens, I return. The eldest (as I said) presides over the family. Wives are ministers to their husbands, children to their parents, and, in general, the younger to the elder. Every city is divided into four equal quarters. In the center of each quarter is a marketplace for all goods. To this place, the products of each family are brought to certain warehouses, where each species of goods is distributed separately. From these, every head of a household seeks whatever he and his own have need of, and he carries it away without money and without any payment whatsoever. For why should anything be denied? Since there is an abundance of all things, there is no fear that anyone might wish to ask for more than is needed. For why would anyone be thought to seek superfluous things when he is certain that he will never lack anything?

This passage describes the economic distribution system in Utopia, where goods are held in common warehouses and distributed to citizens based on need rather than monetary exchange.

Thus, an idle crowd of servants may be excluded.
A return to the citizens. The oldest (as I said) is the head of the family. Servants are the wives of the husbands, and the children of the parents, and in the end, the youngest by nature than the elders. The city is divided into four equal parts. In the middle of each part is a forum, the place of all things. There, in certain houses, the work of each family is gathered together, and in the granaries, each kind of food is separately stored. From these, each head of the family, who himself and his own have need of work, takes what he wants, and takes it without money, without any hostile resistance, whatever he has asked for. Why would anything be denied? Since there is more than enough of all things, and there is no fear that anyone would want more than he needs? For why should he be thought to be seeking in vain, who has certain knowledge that nothing will ever be lacking to him?

Thus, an idle crowd of servants can be excluded.
I return to the citizens. The most ancient (as I have said) is the head of the family. The servants are the wives to the husbands, and the children to the parents, and in the highest degree, the younger to the older. The whole city is divided into four equal parts. In the middle of each part is a forum, the center of all things. In it, the labor of each family is gathered into certain houses, and in the granaries, individual types are distributed separately. From these, any head of the household, who has need of his own and his family, asks, and without money, without any hostility at all, whatever he has asked for, he takes. For why is anything denied? Since there is more than enough of all things, and no fear lies beneath that anyone might wish to demand more than is needed? For why would he be thought to seek superfluous things, who has a certainty that nothing will ever be lacking to him?

For it is against the dignitie of a kynge to haue rule ouer beggers, but rather ouer ryche and welthie men. Of thys mynde was the hardie and couragius Fabrice, when he sayde that he had rather be a ruler of ryche men then be ryche hymselfe. And verelye one man to lyue in pleasure and wealth, whyles all other wepe and smarte for it, that is the parte not of a kynge but of a iayler.
'To be shorte, as he is a folyshe phisition, that cannot cure his patientes disease, onles he caste hym in an other syckenes; so he that cannot amend the liues of his subiectes, but be taking from them the wealth and commoditie of lyfe, he must nedes graunte that he knoweth not the feate howe to gouerne fre men. But let hym rather amende hys owne lyfe, renounce vnhonest pleasures, and forsake pride. For thies be the chiefe vices that cause hym to runne in the contempt or hatered of his people. Let him lyue of hys owne, hurtinge no man. Let him do coste not aboue his power. Let hym restreyne wyckednes. Let hym preuente vices, and take a waye the occasions of offences be well orderyng his subiectes, and not by sufferyng wickednes to increase, afterward to be punyshed. Let hym not be to hastie in callynge agayne lawes, whiche a custome hathe abrogated; speciallye suche as haue bene long forgotten and neuer lacked nor neaded. And let hym neuer vnder the cloke and pretence of transgression take suche fynes and forfaytes, as no iudge wyll suffre a priuate persone to take, as uniuste and ful of gile.

OF THOMAS MORE'S UTOPIA

it is for the dignity of a ruler to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and fortunate. Indeed, Fabricius, a man of an upright and lofty spirit, surely understood this when he replied that he would rather rule over rich men than be rich himself. And in truth, for one person to wallow in pleasure and luxury while others everywhere are groaning and lamenting is to be the jailer, not the ruler, of a kingdom. Finally, just as a most unskilled physician is one who knows not how to cure one disease except by another, so he who does not know how to reform the life of his citizens except by taking away the comforts of life should admit that he does not know how to rule over free men. Rather, let him cast off his own sloth or arrogance; for it is usually through these vices that the people either despise him or hold him in hatred. Let him live innocently upon his own resources, let him adapt his expenses to his revenues, let him curb wrongdoing, and by the right training of his people, let him prevent evils from growing rather than allow them to increase only to punish them later. Let him not rashly revive laws abrogated by custom, especially those which, having been long neglected, were never missed. Nor should he ever accept, in the name of a transgression, anything of a kind that a judge would not allow a private citizen to accept, regarding it as dishonest and cunning. Here, if I were to propose to them the law of the Macarenses, who themselves are not very far from Utopia, whose king, on the first day he begins his reign, after great sacrifices, is bound by an oath never to hold at one time more than a thousand pounds of gold in his treasury, or an equivalent amount in silver. They say this law was established by a certain excellent king, who cared more for the benefit of his country than

The remarkable law of the Macarenses

More argues that a true king secures his authority by managing the welfare of his subjects rather than impoverishing them, and he cites the restrictive wealth laws of the Macarenses as an ideal model of governance.
Fabricius, Macarenses, Utopia, royal duty, poverty, wealth, law, governance

It is a mark of dignity to rule over the poor, rather than over the rich and happy. Indeed, the noble and lofty-spirited Fabricius certainly felt this, and when asked, preferred to rule over the rich, rather than to be rich. And truly, one who flows with pleasures and delights, while others weep and lament, is not a ruler, but a jailer. Furthermore, just as an unskilled physician is unable to cure a disease unless he knows the disease, so too is one who does not correct the citizens' lives by any other means than by the correction of their lives, and who, having lost the benefits of life, confesses that he does not know how to rule the free. Rather, he should either change his own way of life through laziness, or through pride. For these vices often lead to the people either despising him or hating him. Let him live innocently from his own means, adjust his expenses to his income, restrain his pleasures, and rather than allow them to grow, let him prevent them, for they will later punish him. Let him not hastily recall laws that have been abolished, especially those that have long been neglected, for they have never been desired. Nor should he take any commission in the name of such matters, as a private judge, for he would not suffer to receive an unjust and corrupt bribe. If he were to place this law of Macares, which is said to have been established by the best of kings, who cared more for the convenience of his country than for wealth, and who, on the first day he sees the kingdom, binds himself with great sacrifices and oaths, never to place more than a thousand pounds of gold or silver, or as much silver as the gold is worth, in the treasury. This law is said to have been established by a most excellent king, who cared more for the convenience of his country than for wealth.

...is a mark of dignity to exercise command over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and the happy. This very thing Fabricius, a man of erect and sublime spirit, certainly felt when he replied that he would rather command the rich than be rich. And indeed, to be the keeper of a kingdom while others groan and lament on all sides for the sake of some pleasure and delights is not to be the keeper of a kingdom, but of a prison. Finally, just as a physician is most unskilled who does not know how to cure a disease except with disease, so he who does not know how to correct the life of citizens by any other way than by taking away the conveniences of life, confesses that he does not know how to command the free. Rather, he should change his own inertia or pride. For it happens to these vices that the people either despise him or hold him in hatred. Let him live innocently from his own resources, let him accommodate expenses to revenues, let him curb the evils of the people, and let him prevent them from growing by right instruction rather than allowing them to increase, which he will then punish. Let him not rashly recall laws abrogated by custom, especially those which have long been neglected and never desired. Nor should he ever take anything by the name of commission that a private judge would not suffer to be received, as if it were unjust and wicked. If I were to propose to them the law of Macaronesia, which they themselves are not far from Utopia, whose king, on the first day he is inaugurated into the command, is bound by an oath with great sacrifices, that he will never hold more than one thousand pounds of gold, or as much silver as the price of that gold is worth. They say this law was instituted by a certain excellent king, who had greater care for the convenience of the fatherland than for riches.

[context] And whosoever will strive with thee in the law, and take from thee thy coat, yield up to him also thy cloak or mantle.
And whosoever shall compel thee to go with him one mile, go with him two more other. Love your enemies, and do good to them which hate you, and pray for them which persecute you and pick matters against you, that ye may be the sons of your father which is in heaven, which maketh the sun to rise upon good and evil, and sendeth rain upon just and unjust. Thou answerest, he spake not this to me, he spake it to his apostles, he spake it to perfect persons. Heardest thou not how he said that ye may be the sons of your father? if thou care not to be the son of God, that law pertaineth not to thee. Nevertheless he is not good verily which would not be perfect. Hark also another thing: if thou desire no reward, the commandment belongeth not to thee: for it followeth. If ye love them which love you, what reward shall ye have? as who should say, none: for verily, to do these things (that is to say, to love them that loveth thee) is not virtue: but not to do it, is an evil thing: there is debt of neither side where is just recompense made of both sides. Hear Paul, both a great wise man and cunning and an interpreter also of Christ's law. Bless (saith he) them that persecute you, bless them, and curse them in no wise, rendering to no man evil for evil, if it may be as much as in you is, having rest and peace with all men, not defending yourself, my best beloved brethren, but give place and withstand ye not wrath: for it is written, Vengeance shall be reserved to me and I will requite them saith our Lord. But if thine enemy shall be hungry, give to him meat: if he be athirst, give to him drink: for if thou do this, thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, that is to say, thou shalt make him to love fervently. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil in goodness. What shall then follow, sayest thou, if I shall with my softness nourish up the knappyshnes or malice and froward audacity of another man, and in suffering an old injury provoke a new? If thou can without thine own evil either avoid or put by evil, no man forbiddeth thee to do it: but if not, look thou say not, it is better to do than to suffer. Amend thine enemy if thou can, either lading him with benefits, or overcoming him with meekness: if that help not, it is better that the one perish than both: it is better that thou wax rich with the lucre and advantage of patience than that while either to other rendereth evil both be made evil. Let this therefore be a decree among Christian men, to compare with all men in love, in meekness, and in benefits, or doing good: but in striving, hate or backbiting, in rebukes and injury, to give place ever to them that be of lowest degree, and that with good will. But he is unworthy to whom a good turn should be done, or an evil forgiven, yet is it meet for thee to do it, and Christ is worthy for whose sake it is done. I will neither (say they) hurt any man, neither suffer myself to be hurt: yet when thou art hurt, see thou forgive the trespass with all thy heart, providing always that nothing be which any man should remit or forgive unto thee.

[context] Ca. Why in such Haste? Stay a little; pray stay. I'll put on my better Looks, and we'll be merry together.
Eu. What Sort of Cattle have we got here?
Ca. 'Tis the Patriarch of the College: Don't go away, they have had their Dose of Fuddle: Stay but a little While, and as soon as he is gone, we will discourse as we use to do.
Eu. Well, I'll be so good natur'd as to hearken to you, though you would not to me. Now we are alone, you must tell me the whole Story, I would fain have it from your Mouth.
Ca. Now I have found by Experience, of all my Friends, which I took to be very wise Men too, that no Body gave more wise and grave Advice than you, that are the youngest of 'em all.
Eu. Tell me, how did you get your Parents Consent at last?
Ca. First, by the restless Sollicitations of the Monks and Nuns, and then by my own Importunities and Tears, my Mother was at length brought over; but my Father stood out stiffly still: But at last being ply'd by several Engines, he was prevail'd upon to yield; but yet, rather like one that was forced, than that consented. The Matter was concluded in their Cups, and they preach'd Damnation to him, if he refus'd to let Christ have his Spouse.
Eu. O the Villany of Fools! But what then?
Ca. I was kept close at Home for three Days; but in the mean Time there were always with me some Women of the College that they call Convertites, mightily encouraging me to persist in my holy Resolution, and watching me narrowly, lest any of my Friends or Kindred should come at me, and make me alter my Mind. In the mean While, my Habit was making ready, and the Provision for the Feast.
Eu. How did you find yourself? Did not your Mind misgive you yet?
Ca. No, not at all; and yet I was so horridly frighted, that I had rather die ten Times over, than suffer the same again.
Eu. What was that, pray?
Ca. It is not to be uttered.
Eu. Come, tell me freely, you know I'm your Friend.
Ca. Will you keep Counsel?
Eu. I should do that without promising, and I hope you know me better than to doubt of it.

fatim. <term>EV.</term> Quas aves heic video? <term>CA.</term> Est collegii patriarcha. Ne subducito te; jam potarunt; accumbe paullisper; illo digresso fabulabimur nostro more. <term>EV.</term> Age obtestabor tibi, quæ mihi noluisti. Nunc soli sumus, narra totam fabulam, malim enim ex te cognoscere. <term>CA.</term> Ex tot amicis, quos putabam pere plurimum, nunc sentio nullum fuisse, qui mihi prudentius ac senilius consilium dederit, quam tu omnium natu minimus. <term>EV.</term> Sed quo modo expugnasti parentum affectum? <term>CA.</term> Primum improbis hortatibus monachorum, ac monacharum: deinde etiam meis: precibus ac blandimentis labefactus est matris animus: pater nullo pacto quibat perpelli. Tandem omnibus admotis machinis & hic victus & oppressus est potius, quam assensit. Factum est inter pocula: minitabantur horribile malum exitium, si Christo suam sponsam denegaret. <term>EV.</term> O improbitatem stolidorum! Quid fit deinde? <term>CA.</term> Servor triduo domi clam: interim semper aderant mulieres aliquot ejus collegii, quas illi Conversas vocant, hortatibus addentes animum, ut persisterem in sancto proposito, ac solicite caventes, ne qua cognatarum, aut sodalium adiret me, quæ mentem videretur mutatura. Interim adornabantur vestes, aliaque quæ ad convivium attinebant. <term>EV.</term> Tibi quid interim erat animi? Num vacillabas? <term>CA.</term> Non, sed passa sum quiddam tam horrendum, ut malim emori decies, quam iterum perpeti. <term>EV.</term> Quæso, quid istuc est? <term>CA.</term> Non possum effari. <term>EV.</term> Quod mihi dixeris, amico tuo dixeris. <term>CA.</term> Promittis silentium? <term>EV.</term> Id præstaturus eram, etiam si nihil fuisses stipulata. Quasi vero me nondum noris.

EV. What birds do I see here? CA. It is the patriarch of the college. Do not withdraw yourself; they have already had their drink; lie down for a little while; once he has departed, we shall converse in our usual manner. EV. Come, I beseech you, tell me what you refused me before. Now that we are alone, tell the whole story, for I would rather learn it from you. CA. Out of so many friends, whom I thought to be of the utmost value, I now realize there was not one who gave me more prudent and mature advice than you, the youngest of all. EV. But in what manner did you overcome the affection of your parents? CA. First, through the wicked exhortations of the monks and nuns; then, my mother’s mind was shaken by my own prayers and blandishments. My father could in no way be compelled. Finally, with all manner of devices brought to bear, he was conquered and overwhelmed, rather than persuaded. It was done over the wine cups; they threatened horrific and wretched ruin if he denied his daughter to Christ. EV. Oh, the wickedness of the foolish! What happened next? CA. I was kept hidden at home for three days; meanwhile, certain women of that college, whom they call Conversas, were always present, adding spirit to my resolve with their exhortations and anxiously taking care that no relative or companion should approach me who might seem capable of changing my mind. In the meantime, the clothes and other things belonging to the feast were being prepared. EV. What was your state of mind meanwhile? Did you waver? CA. No, but I suffered something so horrendous that I would rather die ten times than endure it again. EV. I ask you, what is that? CA. I cannot speak it. EV. What you have said to me, you have said to your friend. CA. Do you promise silence? EV. I would have provided that, even if you had stipulated nothing. As if you did not know me yet.

Catharina recounts the intense psychological pressure and manipulation by monks and nuns used to force her into religious life, despite her father's initial resistance.

Fatim. EV. What birds do I see here? CA. It is the patriarch of the college. Do not be discouraged; they have already drunk; rest for a little while; when he is gone, we will talk as we usually do. EV. Then I will beg you, tell me what you refused to tell me. Now we are alone, tell me the whole story; I would rather learn it from you. CA. Among all the friends I thought I had most, now I feel that none of them gave me wiser or more mature advice than you, the smallest in nature among all. EV. But how did you overcome your parents' affection? CA. First, by the improper encouragement of monks and nuns; then, even more so, by my own prayers and flattery. The mother's spirit was weakened, and the father would not allow himself to be persuaded in any way. Finally, after all the schemes had been set in motion, he was conquered and crushed rather than consenting. It happened during a drinking session: they threatened a terrible fate if he refused to give his daughter in marriage to Christ. EV. O the stupidity of these villains! What happened next? CA. I remained at home for three days in secret; meanwhile, several women of that college, whom they call Conversas, were always present, encouraging me to remain steadfast in my holy purpose, and carefully watching, so that no one, whether known or familiar, would come to me, for they thought my mind might change. Meanwhile, the clothes were being prepared, and other things necessary for the banquet. EV. What was your state of mind in the meantime? Were you wavering? CA. No, but I endured something so terrible that I would rather die ten times than go through it again. EV. Please, what was that? CA. I cannot speak of it. EV. Whatever you tell me, you will tell my friend. CA. Do you promise silence? EV. I was ready to promise it even if you had not asked. As if you did not yet know me.

they almost adopt the notion of the Manichæans, that the God of the Old Testament is a different being from the God of the New. But we shall easily get rid of such difficulties, if we direct our attention to that dispensation of God, which I have observed; namely, that during that period, in which he gave the Israelites his covenant involved in some degree of obscurity, he intended to signify and prefigure the grace of future and eternal felicity by terrestrial blessings, and the grievousness of spiritual death by corporal punishments.
IV. Another difference between the Old Testament and the New consists in figures, because the former, in the absence of the truth, displayed merely an image and shadow instead of the body; but the latter exhibits the present truth and the substantial body. And this is generally mentioned wherever the New Testament is opposed to the Old, but is treated more at large in the Epistle to the Hebrews than in any other place. The apostle is there disputing against those who supposed that the observance of the Mosaic law could not be abolished, without being followed by the total ruin of religion. To refute this error, he adduces the prediction of the psalmist concerning the priesthood of Christ; for since he has an eternal priesthood committed to him, we may argue the certain abolition of that priesthood, in which new priests daily succeeded each other. But he proves the superiority of the appointment of this new Priest, because it is confirmed with an oath. He afterwards adds that this transfer of the priesthood implies also a change of the covenant. And he proves that this change was necessary, because such was the imbecility of the law, that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to state the nature of this imbecility; namely, that the law prescribed external righteousnesses, consisting in carnal ordinances, which could not make the observers of them “perfect as pertaining to the conscience,” that by animal victims it could neither expiate sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it contained “a shadow of good things to come, but not the very image of the things;” and that consequently it had no other office, but to serve as an introduction to “a better hope,” which is exhibited in the gospel. Here we have to inquire in what respect the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical, the ministry of Christ with the ministry of Moses. For if the comparison related to the substance of the promises, there would be a great discordance between the two testaments; but as the state of the question leads us to a different point, we must attend to the scope of the apostle, in order to discover the truth. Let us, then, bring forward the covenant, which God has once made, which is eternal, and never to be abolished. The accomplishment, whence it derives its establishment and ratification, is Christ. While such a confirmation was waited for, the Lord by Moses prescribed ceremonies, to serve as solemn symbols of the confirmation. It came to be a subject of contention, whether the ceremonies ordained in the law ought to cease and give place to Christ. Now, though these ceremonies were only accidents or concomitants of the covenant, yet being the instruments of its administration, they bear the name of the covenant; as it is common to give to other sacraments the names of the things they represent. In a word, therefore, what is here called the Old Testament is a solemn method of confirming the covenant, consisting of ceremonies and sacrifices. Since it contains nothing substantial, unless we proceed further, the apostle contends that it ought to be repealed and abrogated, in order to make way for Christ, the Surety and Mediator of a better testament, by whom eternal sanctification has been at once procured for the elect, and those transgressions obliterated, which remained under the law. Or, if you prefer it, take the following statement of it; that the Old Testament of the Lord was that which was delivered to the Jews, involved in a shadowy and inefficacious observance of ceremonies, and that it was therefore temporary, because it remained as it were in suspense, till it was supported by a firm and substantial confirmation; but that it was made new and eternal, when it was consecrated and established by the blood of Christ. Whence Christ calls the cup which he gives to his disciples in the supper, “the cup of the New Testament in his blood;” to signify that when the testament of God is sealed with his blood, the truth of it is then accomplished, and thus it is made new and eternal.
V. Hence it appears in what sense the apostle said, that the Jews were conducted to Christ by the tuition of the law, before he was manifested in the flesh. He confesses also that they were children and heirs of God, but such as, on account of their age, required to be kept under the care of a tutor. For it was reasonable that before the Sun of Righteousness was risen, there should be neither such a full blaze of revelation, nor such great clearness of understanding. Therefore the Lord dispensed the light of his word to them in such a manner, that they had yet only a distant and obscure prospect of it. Paul describes this slenderness of understanding as a state of childhood, which it was the Lord’s will to exercise in the elements of this world and in external observances, as rules of puerile discipline, till the manifestation of Christ, by whom the knowledge of the faithful was to grow to maturity. Christ himself alluded to this distinction, when he said, “The law and the prophets were until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached.” What discoveries did Moses and the prophets make to their contemporaries? They afforded them some taste of that wisdom which was in after times to be clearly manifested, and gave them a distant prospect of its future splendour. But when Christ could be plainly pointed out, the kingdom of God was revealed. For in him are discovered “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” by which we penetrate almost into the furthest recesses of heaven.

nichæis accidit. Verùm talibus scrupulis facilè expediemur si animū referemus ad istam quam notaui Dei dispensationem, quòd tum futuræ ac æternæ fœlicitatis gratiam terrestribus beneficiis, tum spiritualis mortis grauitatem corporeis pœnis significare & figura-re pro eo tempore voluit quo Testamētum suum quodammodo adhuc inuolutum Israeli-tico populo tradebat.

4 Alterum Veteris & Noui testamenti discrimen statuitur in figuris, quòd illud absente veritate, imaginem tantùm & pro corpore vmbram ostentabat: hoc præsentem veritatem & corpus solidū exhibet. Atque huius fere fit mentio vbicunque veteri testamento nouum opponitur: fusior tamen est eius tractatio in epistola ad Hebræos quàm alibi vsquam. Illic disputat Apostolus aduersus eos qui Legis Mosaicæ obseruationes aboleri posse non puta-bant nisi vt secum traherent religionis totius ruinam. Quo hunc errorem refutet, assumit <margin>Psal. 110. b. 4</margin> quod de Christi sacerdotio prædictum apud Prophetam fuerat. nam quum æternum illi deferatur sacerdotium, certū est aboleri sacerdotium illud vbi alii aliis successores quoti-die substituebantur. Præualere autem noui istius sacerdotis institutionem probat, quòd <margin>Heb. 7. b. 11. c. 19. & 9. c. 9. & 10. a. 1</margin> iuramento stabilitur. Subiungit postea, in ea sacerdotii translatione verti etiam Testamē-ti mutationem. Atque id necessarium fuisse ratione cōfirmat, quoniam ea erat Legis im-becillitas quæ nihil adducere ad perfectionē posset. Tum deinde prosequitur quæ illa fue-rit imbecillitas, nēpe quòd externas carnis iustitias habuerit quæ cultores suos non possēt secundū conscientiam perfectos reddere, quòd pecudum victimis, nec peccata delere, nec veram sanctitatem conciliare poterat. Concludit ergo, vmbram fuisse in ipsa futurorum bonorum, non viuam rerum effigiem: ideoque non aliud habuisse officii nisi vt introdu-ctio esset in spem meliorem quæ in Euangelio exhibetur. Hic videndum est qua parte fœ-dus Legale cum fœdere Euangelico, Christi ministerium cum Mosaico conferatur. Nam si ad promissionum substantiam pertineret comparatio, magnum extaret inter duo Testa-menta dissidium: sed quum status quæstionis aliò nos ducat, eò tendendum est vt verū re-periamus. Fœdus ergo quod æternum & nunquam interiturum semel sanciuit, in medio statuamus. Illius complementum, vnde tandem habet vt statum ratúmque sit, Christus est. Talis confirmatio dum expectatur, ceremonias Dominus per Mosen præscribit, quæ sunt velut solennia confirmationis symbola. Id in contentionem veniebat, cederéne oporteret Christo quæ in Lege ordinatæ erant ceremoniæ. Hæ verò tametsi fœderis duntaxat acci-dentia erant, vel certè accessiones ac annexa, & (vt vulgus loquitur) accessoria: quia tamen instrumenta erant illius administrandi, fœderis nomen habent. qualiter & aliis Sacramē-tis dari solet. Proinde, in summa, Vetus testamentum hoc loco appellatur solennis confir-mandi fœderis ratio, ceremoniis & sacrificiis cōprehensa. En ia quoniā nihil solidū subest, nisi vlterius transeatur, oportuisse antiquari & abrogari cōtendit Apostolus, vt Christo po-tioris Testamenti sponsori ac mediatori locus daretur, per quem æterna sanctificatio ele-ctis semel acquisita est: & transgressiones obliteratæ, quæ sub Lege manebant. Quòd si ma-lis, ita accipe: vetus fuisse Domini Testamentum, quod vmbratili & inefficaci ceremonia-rum obseruatione inuolutum tradebatur. ideoque temporarium fuisse, quia veluti in su-spenso erat, donec firma & substantiali confirmatione subniteretur. Tum verò demū no-uum æternúmque factum fuisse, postquam Christi sanguine consecratum stabilitúmque fuit. Vnde calicem, quem discipulis in Cœna porrigit Christus, Noui testamenti calicem <margin>Matt. 26. c. 28</margin> vocat in suo sanguine: vt significet, tum verè Dei Testamento suam constare veritatē, per quam nouum fit & æternum dum sanguine suo obsignatur.

5 Hinc liquet quo sensu dixerit Apostolus, Legis pædagogia deductos fuisse Iudæos ad <margin>Galat. 3. d. 24. & 4. a. 1</margin> Christum antequam ipse in carne exhiberetur. Illos quoque filios & hæredes Dei fuisse fa-tetur: sed qui propter pueritiam sub pædagogi custodia habendi essent. Cōueniebat enim, sole iustitiæ nondum exorto, nec tantum esse reuelationis fulgorem, nec tantā intelligen-di perspicaciam. Sic ergo verbi sui lucem illis Dominus dispensauit, vt eam eminus adhuc & obscurè cernerent. Ideo hanc intelligentiæ tenuitatem pueritiæ vocabulo Paulus notat, quā elementis huius mundi & externis obseruatiūculis, tanquā regulis puerilis disciplinæ, voluit Dominus exerceri, donec effulgeret Christus: per quē fidelis populi cognitionē ado-lescere oportebat. Hanc distinctionem signauit Christus ipse, quum diceret, Legem & Pro- <margin>Matth. 11. b. 13</margin> phetas fuisse vsque ad Iohannem: ex eo euangelizari regnum Dei. Quid Lex & Prophetæ sui temporis hominibus prodiderūt? nempe gustum præbebant eius sapientiæ quæ olim ad liquidum manifestanda erat, & procul emicantem præmonstrābant. Vbi autem digito potest ostendi Christus, referatum est regnum Dei. In ipso enim expositi sunt thesauri o- <margin>Coloss. 2. b. 9</margin> mnes sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, quibus propè ad ipsa cæli adyta penetratur.

it happens. But we shall easily be disentangled from such scruples if we turn our mind to that dispensation of God which I have noted, that he wished at that time to signify and figure both the grace of future and eternal happiness by earthly benefits, and the gravity of spiritual death by bodily punishments, for that time when he was delivering his Testament, still in some way wrapped up, to the Israelite people.

4 Another difference between the Old and New Testaments is established in the figures, in that the former, with the truth absent, showed only an image and a shadow instead of the body, whereas the latter exhibits the present truth and a solid body. And mention of this is made almost everywhere the New Testament is opposed to the Old, yet its treatment is more extensive in the Epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There, the Apostle disputes against those who thought that the observances of the Mosaic Law could not be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the entire religion. To refute this error, he assumes Psalm 110:4 what had been predicted by the Prophet concerning the priesthood of Christ. For since an eternal priesthood is bestowed upon him, it is certain that the priesthood in which others were substituted as successors to others every day was to be abolished. Furthermore, he proves the pre-eminence of the institution of this new priest by the fact that it is established by an oath Hebrews 7:11, 19; 9:9; 10:1. He adds afterward that in that translation of the priesthood, there is also a change of the Testament. And he confirms that this was necessary by reason, since the weakness of the Law was such that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to explain what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justices of the flesh which could not make its worshippers perfect according to conscience, and that through the victims of beasts, it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it was a shadow in the very thing of future goods, not a living image of the things, and that therefore it had no other duty than to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. Here we must see in what part the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, and the ministry of Christ with the Mosaic. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, there would be a great disagreement between the two Testaments, but since the status of the question leads us elsewhere, we must tend toward finding the truth. Let us, therefore, place in the middle the covenant which God ratified once and for all as eternal and never to perish. The completion of that covenant, from which it finally derives its status as ratified and firm, is Christ. While such confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are like solemn symbols of confirmation. This came into contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. Although these were merely accidents of the covenant, or certainly accessions and annexes, and (as the common people say) accessories, yet because they were instruments of administering it, they have the name of the covenant, just as it is accustomed to be given to other Sacraments. Therefore, in sum, the Old Testament is called in this place the solemn method of confirming the covenant, comprised in ceremonies and sacrifices. Since nothing solid underlies it unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be antiquated and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the sponsor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification was acquired once for all for the elect, and transgressions were obliterated, which remained under the Law. But if you prefer it so, take it thus: the Old Testament was the Lord's, which was delivered wrapped up in the shadowy and ineffective observance of ceremonies, and therefore it was temporary, because it was, as it were, in suspense until it was supported by a firm and substantial confirmation. But then it was finally made new and eternal, after it was consecrated and stabilized by the blood of Christ. Whence the cup which Christ holds out to his disciples in the Supper, he calls the cup of the New Testament Matthew 26:28 in his blood, to signify that the Testament of God then truly attains its own truth, through which it becomes new and eternal, while it is sealed by his blood.

5 From this, it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that the Jews were led by the pedagogy of the Law to Christ Galatians 3:24; 4:1 before he himself was exhibited in the flesh. He acknowledges that they were also children and heirs of God, but who, because of childhood, had to be kept under the custody of a tutor. For it was fitting that, the sun of justice not yet having risen, there should be neither such splendor of revelation nor such perspicacity of understanding. Thus, therefore, the Lord dispensed the light of his Word to them, so that they might see it from afar and still obscurely. Therefore, Paul marks this thinness of intelligence with the word childhood, which the Lord willed to be exercised by the elements of this world and external little observances, as if they were rules of childish discipline, until Christ should shine forth, through whom it was necessary that the cognition of the faithful people should mature. Christ himself marked this distinction when he said that the Law and the Prophets were until John, and from that time the kingdom of God is evangelized Matthew 11:13. What did the Law and the Prophets profit the men of their time? Namely, they provided a taste of that wisdom which was one day to be manifested clearly, and they prefigured it shining from afar. But where Christ can be pointed out with the finger, the kingdom of God is laid open. For in him are deposited all the treasures of wisdom and intelligence Colossians 2:9, by which one penetrates near to the very sanctuaries of heaven.

Calvin explains that the Old Testament ceremonies were temporary, shadowy figures intended to lead the people toward the eventual perfection found in Christ, who established the New Testament through his blood.

However, we can easily deal with such concerns if we refer our minds to this particular dispensation of God, which was that, at that time, the grace of future and eternal happiness was signified and represented by earthly benefits, and the weight of spiritual death was shown and figured by bodily punishments, for that was the time when His covenant was being given to the Israelite people, somewhat still wrapped up.

4 The distinction between the Old and New Testament is established in figures, for the Old Testament, in the absence of truth, only showed an image and a shadow of the body; this one, however, presents the present truth and a solid body. Mention of this is made almost everywhere the Old Testament is opposed to the New, but the treatment is more detailed in the letter to the Hebrews than elsewhere. There, the Apostle disputes against those who thought that the observance of the Mosaic Law could be abolished without bringing about the ruin of the whole religion. To refute this error, he cites Psalm 110, verse 4, which had been spoken of Christ's priesthood by the Prophet. For when an eternal priesthood is given to Him, it is certain that the priesthood which had other successors every day must be abolished. He proves that the institution of this new priesthood prevails, because it is established by an oath. He then adds that in this transfer of priesthood, there is also a change of covenant. And he confirms that this was necessary, because the Law was weak and could not bring anything toward perfection. Then he proceeds to explain what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justifications of the flesh, which could not make its worshippers perfect in conscience, nor could it remove sins, nor could it bring about true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that the shadow was of the future good things, not the true image of things; thus, it had no other office than to be an introduction to the better hope which is set forth in the Gospel. Here it is to be noted how the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, Christ's ministry with the Mosaic. For if the comparison were about the substance of promises, there would be a great difference between the two covenants; but since the question leads us in another direction, we must seek the truth. The covenant which was once established as eternal and never to be annulled stands in the middle. Christ is the one who completes it, giving it a settled and ratified status. While this confirmation is awaited, the Lord, through Moses, prescribes ceremonies, which are like symbols of solemn confirmation. This came up in the dispute about whether it was necessary to yield to Christ what was ordered in the Law. These ceremonies, however, were merely incidental to the covenant, or rather, additions and accessories, and (as the common people say) supplementary matters; yet, since they were instruments for administering the covenant, they are called by the name of the covenant. Just as other sacraments are given. Therefore, in summary, the Old Testament is here called the solemn way of confirming the covenant, including ceremonies and sacrifices. Since nothing solid is present, except to go further, the Apostle argues that it was necessary to make the Old Testament antiquated and abolished, so that the place of Christ, as the sponsor and mediator of a better covenant, might be given to Him, through whom the eternal sanctification of the chosen was once obtained, and the transgressions that remained under the Law were blotted out. If you do not like it, take it this way: the Old Testament of the Lord was given wrapped up in a shadowy and ineffective observance of ceremonies. Therefore, it was temporary, because it was as if suspended, until it was confirmed with a firm and substantial agreement. Then, indeed, the New and eternal covenant was made, after Christ's blood had consecrated and established it. Hence, the cup which Christ gives to his disciples at the Supper, He calls the cup of the New Testament, in His own blood, to signify that His covenant with God is indeed true, by which the new and eternal covenant is made when it is signed with His blood.

5 From this it is clear that the Apostle meant that the Jews were led by the pedagogy of the Law to Christ before He was revealed in the flesh. He also acknowledges that they were the children and heirs of God, but that they were still under the care of a tutor because of their youth. For it was fitting, while the sole justice had not yet arisen, and neither was there a full revelation nor such a clear understanding. Thus, the Lord dispensed the light of His word to them in such a way that they could still see it only dimly and obscurely. Therefore, Paul notes this weakness of understanding by the term "youth," for by means of the elements of this world and external observances, like the rules of childish discipline, the Lord wished to train them until Christ would appear, through whom the knowledge of the faithful people would grow. Christ Himself marked this distinction when He said, "The Law and the Prophets were until John," from which the kingdom of God was to be proclaimed. What did the Law and the Prophets of His time reveal to men? Namely, they gave a taste of the wisdom that was to be clearly revealed later, and they foretold the coming of Christ. When Christ could be shown by a finger, the kingdom of God was proclaimed. For in Him are revealed the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, by which one is nearly able to enter the very innermost parts of heaven.

I HAVE unfolded all my forces and my discourse, Lipsius; and you have what I deemed ought to be said in favor of Constancy against Sorrow. They will help, however, if you let them sink not just into your ears, but into your mind; and if you do not allow these things to lie there and wither after being heard, like seeds scattered on the surface of the soil. There is, under the rule, a peaceful sex. Gaul? Look and pity. Even now, through all its articles, a gangrenous wound spreads from the bloody war. Nor is it otherwise throughout the whole world. Consider this, Lipsius; and through this common suffering, lighten your burdens. And just as a servant, who is left behind by the triumphant, is accustomed to cry out amidst the joy of the triumph, "Man am I!" so let this warning always stand by you, "To be this human." ### On the shame felt from undeserved praise.
## D I A L. XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unworthily,
> If you condemn again, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* You are accused of having praised an unworthy man. Truly, that which is evil often springs from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they are themselves, imagine others to be the same. Hence, they are even more prone to praise; and although I admit that to praise an unworthy person is a mistake, it is still much worse to disparage one who is undeserving.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did it knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if you did it through ignorance, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another, but to deceive is the crime belonging to the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another reflects upon my own infamy.

*Reason.* Rather, it reflects your own fault or ignorance. For there is no infamy in the praise of another, just as there is no glory in it.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly to have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* See to it, therefore, that you do not grieve over this very thing often. Beware of rushing rashly into praising or blaming. For there is an urge for both, and (to speak precisely) a disease and a certain itch of a tongue that is restless and ignorant of quiet, the bridle and guard of which are counted among the works of the highest perfection, as Scripture says:

### On the shame of being praised by unworthy people.
## Dialogue XXVI.

> Be sparing in praise, for when you are praised unjustly,
> If you again condemn, a part of lightness will be there.

*Do.* It is unjust to praise.

A large ornamental initial L at the start of the dialogue response.
*Ra.* It is indeed unjust to praise. Although it is a bad thing, it often arises from a good root. The good and the innocent, who are such themselves, think others are the same. From this, they are even more inclined to praise. And although it is wrong to praise something bad, I admit it: yet it is much worse to condemn something unworthy.

*Do.* I praised something unworthy.

*Ra.* If you do so knowingly, it is reprehensible; but if you do so unknowingly, it is excusable. It is less bad to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is another's fault; to deceive is the fault of the one who deceives.

*Do.* The praise of another turns to my infamy.

*Ra.* No, indeed, it is either your fault or your ignorance. For from another, as praise is, so infamy is not.

*Do.* To be praised unworthily, I suffer greatly.

*Ra.* Therefore, look that you do not suffer that very thing often. Be careful not to rashly turn to praising and condemning. For there is a desire for both things: and (as I shall say properly) a disease, and a certain itching of the mobile and quiet tongue, of ignorance. Its bridle and its care are counted among the works of the highest perfection, as the Scripture says:

Fortuna, laus, infamia, pudor, virtus, conscientia, Scriptura

...to entice, and say to him: "I suffer these things indeed, O Queen, wishing for you; you will restore me to my whole self, or at least you are enough for me in one thing for all things. You, restore me with your only pious bosom, so that I may not feel the harms of fame, but also of life."

*Do.* I am often torn in the commonplaces of the streets.

*Ra.* A good counselor. The common people will make you known, virtue will make you clear, and conscience will make you secure.

---

### On the shame of seeking praise from unworthy people.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Spare the one being praised, for when you praise someone unjustly,
> If you then condemn them, there will be a part of lightness.

*Do.* I am accused of praising something unworthy.
*Ra.* I am accused of praising something unworthy. It is indeed a bad thing, but it often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they themselves are, think others are the same. Hence, they are also more prone to praising; and although I confess that it is unworthy to praise a bad thing, it is much worse to criticize something that is not deserving.

*Do.* I praised something unworthy.

*Ra.* If you are reproachable for knowing it, but if you are ignorant, you are excusable. It is less bad to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another; but to deceive is the crime of the one deceiving.

*Do.* The praise of another turns into my own infamy.

*Ra.* Indeed, it is either your own fault or your own ignorance. For from another, as there is praise, so there is no infamy.

*Do.* I am greatly grieved that I praised something unworthy.

*Ra.* See, therefore, that you do not grieve for that very thing often. Take care not to rashly expose yourself to praising and criticizing. For there is a lust for both things, and (to speak properly) a disease and a certain itch of the mobile and quiet tongue, which is not counted among the works of excellent perfection, Scripture saying:

[context] These two rules being rightly understood (for extant and non-extant property), the answer will not be difficult to the questions
which are wont to be proposed by Jurists and by Theologians, writing for the instruction of the internal tribunal of the mind.
III. In the first place, it appears that a bona fide possessor is not bound to any restitution, if the thing be destroyed ; for he neither has the thing nor any gain from the thing : [a mala fide possessor is bound by his own act, besides the consequences of wrong doing.]
IV. Secondly, a bona fide possessor is bound to restore also the still extant produce of the thing : I say the produce of the thing ; for the produce of industry, even if it would not take place without the thing, is not due to the thing. The cause of this obligation is ownership : for he who is owner of a thing is naturally owner of the fruits of the thing.
V. Thirdly, that a bona fide possessor is bound to restitution both of the thing and of the produce of it consumed by him, if in any case he would have consumed as much : for by so much he is held to be richer. And accordingly Caligula is praised for having, in the beginning of his reign, when he restored governments to persons, given them also the income of the interval elapsed.
VI. Fourthly, a bona fide possessor is not bound to restore the produce which he neglected to take ; for he neither has the thing, nor anything which has come into its place.
VII. Fifthly, if a bona fide possessor has given to another a thing given to himself, he is not bound to restitution, except, in any case, without having this thing, he would have given something of equal value : for then he has gained by sparing his own property.
VIII. Sixthly, if he sell a thing which he have bought (belonging to another), he is not bound, except in so far as he sold it for more than he gave for it. If he have sold a thing given to him (belonging to another) he is held to restore the price; except it happen that he have spent the price, and would not otherwise have spent the money.
IX. Seventhly, a thing belonging to another which has been bona fide bought, is to be restored, and the price paid cannot be demanded back. To which rule it seems to me that this exception should be made ; — except in so far as the owner could not probably recover possession of his thing without some expense; as, for example, if it were in the hands of pirates : for then we may deduct as much as the owner would willingly have expended on it. For the actual possession of a thing, especially of a thing difficult to recover, is of itself a valuable matter, and in this the owner, after he has lost the thing [and recovered it] is richer than he was before. And therefore though the buying of a thing which is one's own is not valid by ordinary law, yet Paulus says that it is valid, if it be agreed from the first that the possession which another has of it may be bought. III. For it first appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held beyond the account of the thing itself due to his own deed) is not held to any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither is the thing itself with him, nor is there any gain from the thing.

Medina de contr. q. 10. Zeff. l. II. c. 14. Navar. c. 17. n. 7.
IV. Secondly, that a possessor in good faith is held to restore even the existing fruits of the thing: I say the fruits of the thing; for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is from ownership. For he who is the owner of a thing, is naturally the owner of the fruits of that thing.

V. Thirdly, that a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much anyway: for in this he is considered to have become wealthier. Thus C. Caesar Caligula Suet. c. 16. is praised regarding the beginnings of his reign, because he added the fruits of the interim period to those to whom he restored kingdoms.

VI. Fourthly, that he is not held for the fruits which he neglected to gather: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifthly, if such a possessor has donated to another a thing donated to him, he is not held unless he would have donated just as much even without this thing: for then it will be a gain to have spared his own property.

L. Quivæs. §. ult. D. furti.
VIII. Sixthly, if he has sold a thing purchased, he is not held, unless perhaps insofar as he sold it for more: but if he sold a donated thing, he is held to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, having otherwise not intended to squander it.

[context] the monster attacked people it found rather than animals.
Anxiety led to the invention of a means of avenging so much bloodshed. The path it took when leaving its lair at night in search of prey, was carefully studied. The natives cut the road, digging a ditch which they covered over with boughs and earth. The tiger, which was a male, was incautious, and, falling into the ditch, remained there, stuck on the sharp points fixed in the bottom. Its roarings filled the neighbourhood and the mountains echoed with piercing howls. They killed the monster stuck on the points, by throwing great stones from the banks of the ditch. With one blow of its paw it broke the javelins thrown at it into a thousand fragments, and even when dead and no longer breathing, it filled all who beheld him with terror. What would have happened had it been free and unhurt! A civilian called Juan de Ledesma, a friend of Vasco, and his companion in danger, says that he ate the flesh of that tiger; he told me that it was not inferior to beef. When one asks these people who have never seen tigers why they affirm that this beast was a tiger, they reply that it was because it was spotted, ferocious, sly, and offered other characteristics which others have attributed to tigers. Nevertheless the majority of Spaniards affirm that they have seen spotted leopards and panthers.
After the male tiger was killed, they followed its track through the mountains, and discovered the cave where it lived with its family. The female was absent; but two little ones, still unweaned, were lying there, and these the Spaniards carried away; but changing their minds afterwards and wishing to carry them to Spain when they were a little larger, they put carefully riveted chains round their necks and took them back to the cave, in order that their mother might nurse them. Some days later they went back and found the chains still there, but the cave was empty. It is thought the mother, in a fury, tore the little ones to pieces, and took them away, in order that nobody should have them; for they could not possibly have got loose from their chains alive. The dead tiger's skin was stuffed with dried herbs and straw, and sent to Hispaniola to be presented to the Admiral and other officials, from whom the colonists of those two new countries obtain laws and assistance.
This story was told me by those who had suffered from the ravages of that tiger, and had touched its skin; let us accept what they give us.
Let us now return to Pacra, from whom we have somewhat wandered. After having entered the boios (that is to say, the house) abandoned by the cacique, Vasco sought to induce him to return by means of envoys who made known the conditions already proposed to other caciques; but for a long time Pacra refused. Vasco then tried threats, and the cacique finally decided to come in, accompanied by three others. Vasco writes that he was deformed, and so dirty and hideous that nothing more abominable could be imagined. Nature confined herself to giving him a human form, but he is a brute beast, savage and monstrous. His morals were on a par with his bearing and physiognomy. He had carried off the daughters of four neighbouring caciques to satisfy his brutal passions. The neighbouring chiefs, regarding Vasco as a supreme judge or a Hercules, a redresser of injuries, complained of the debaucheries and the crimes of Pacra, begging that he should be punished by death. Vasco had this filthy beast and the other three caciques, who obeyed him and shared his passions, torn to pieces by dogs of war, and the fragments of their bodies were afterwards burnt. Astonishing things are said about these dogs the Spaniards take into battle. These animals throw themselves with fury on the armed natives pointed out to them, as if they were timid deer or fierce boars; and it often happens that there is no need of swords or javelins to rout the enemy. A command is given to these dogs who form the vanguard, and the natives at the mere sight of these formidable Molossians and the unaccustomed sound of their baying, break their ranks and flee as though horrified and stupefied by some unheard-of prodigy. This does not occur in fighting against the natives of Caramaira or the Caribs, who are braver and understand more about war. They shoot their poisoned arrows with the rapidity of lightning, and kill the dogs in great numbers; but the natives of these mountains do not use arrows in warfare; they only use machanes, that is to say, large wooden swords, and lances with burnt points.
While Pacra was still alive they asked him where his people obtained gold, but neither by persuasion nor threats nor tortures could they drag this secret from him. When asked how he had procured what he had possessed,--for he had offered a present of thirty pounds of gold out of his treasury--he answered that those of his subjects who, either in the time of his parents or in his own, had mined that gold in the mountain were dead, and that since his youth he had not troubled to look for gold. Nothing more could be obtained from him on this subject.
The rigorous treatment of Pacra secured Vasco the friendship of the neighbouring caciques,

The narrow paths of the trails by which he was accustomed to go out at night from the shelters of the caves for prey were explored, and the path was cut. They excavated a pit and covered it with hurdles and thrown earth, the excess soil having been dispersed. What about the tiger? When the unsuspecting male tiger came, he fell into the pit and became fixed upon sharp stakes set in the bottom of the pit. With his roaring, he deafened the whole neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with that shrieking. He was killed by huge stones thrown onto him from the edges of the ditch, and by the stakes already fixed in him. He broke the spears aimed and thrown from above into a thousand fragments and a thousand splinters. While half-dead and drained of blood, he still filled those watching with terror, considering what he might have done had he been loose and unharmed. A certain Juan de Ledesma, a man from Seville, a friend and companion in labors of Vasco, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was no worse than beef. When asked, those who saw the tiger where they might say it is a tiger, they reply that they judge it to be a tiger from the spots, from its ferocity, from its dexterity, and from other signs given by the authors, although many of them claim to have seen spotted leopards and panthers themselves. After the tiger was killed, they followed his tracks toward the mountains and reached his den, his conjugal dwelling.

In the absence of the mother, they took two cubs, not yet ready to be weaned. Having changed their plan to send them to Spain once they were grown, they returned the little ones to the mother's den, with iron chains carefully fastened around their necks. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty, with the chains exactly where they had left them. They thought the mother had torn them to pieces out of rage and carried them off, so that no one might enjoy them. For they assert that they could by no means have freed themselves alive from the chains. The skin of the killed tiger was sent to Hispaniola, stuffed with dry herbs and straw, to the Admiral and the leaders from whom these laws and aid for the new lands are expected. The male, coming incautiously, fell into the pit and stuck in the sharp stakes fixed in the bottom of the ditch. He was blinding his entire neighborhood with his roaring, and the mountains echoed with that sound. He was killed by huge stones and stakes fixed in the upper ditch. He broke the stakes, which were fixed on the right, and thrown from a height. He filled the half-dead and bloodless ones with fear, looking at what he had done, being free and unharmed. A certain Juan de Ledesma, a friend and companion of Vasco, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported that the meat was no worse than beef. The tiger, having crossed the mountains, follows the tracks of that one, and reaches the cave, the conjugal home of that one.
Two puppies, while the mother was absent, took the milk from the breasts, which were still unripe. Changing their plan, they sent them to Spain, having made them larger, and having tied them with iron chains to their necks, they brought them back to the maternal cave. After a few days, they returned to the cave, having changed the chains in their place, and found the cave empty. They were carrying the mother, torn into pieces by the rage of the tiger, and taken away, so that no one could enjoy her. For they asserted that they could not have been released from the chains in any way while alive. The skin of the killed tiger, stuffed with herbs and straw, was sent to Spain to the admirals and the nobles, from whom this new land expects laws and help. And those who suffered from the tiger and those who handled its skin told me these things, which we accept as true. We must return to the cave from which we departed. The Vasco, having entered the cave, which is called a house, tries to attract the cave. The cave, which we mentioned as having been signified to others, resisted for a long time. When the threats were rejected, more were added. Finally, he came with three rules as companions. The Vasco writes that the cave is deformed and sordid, and foul, so that it never admits to having seen anything more shameful. He says that nature gave it only human form, but otherwise it is a wild, brutish, and monstrous animal. He says that its habits are equal to its appearance and features. He abuses the daughters of the four neighboring rulers with detestable lust. [context] But let us suppose that St. Peter had directed his Epistle to the Natural born Subjects, and those not private persons neither;
suppose he had writ to the Senate of Rome, What then? No Law that is grounded upon a reason, expresly set down in the Law it self, obligeth further than the reason of it extends. Be subject, says he, ὑποτάγητε : That is, according to the genuine sense and import of the word, be subordinate, or legally subject. For the law, Aristotle says, is order. Submit for the Lord's sake. Why so? Because a King is an Officer appointed by God for the punishment of evil doers, and the praise of them that do well. For so is the will of God: To wit, That we should submit and yield Obedience to such as are here described. There is not a word spoken of any other. You see the ground of this Precept, and how well 'tis laid. The Apostle adds in the 16th v. as Free; therefore not as Slaves. What now, if Princes pervert the design of Magistracy, and use the power that is put into their Hands, to the ruin and destruction of good men; and the praise and encouragement of evil doers? Must we all be condemn'd to perpetual Slavery, not private persons only, but our Nobility, all our inferior Magistrates; our very Parliament it self? Is not temporal Government call'd a humane Ordinance? How comes it to pass then, that mankind should have power to appoint and constitute, what may be good and profitable for one another; and want power to restrain or suppress things that are universally mischievious and destructive? That Prince, you say, whom St. Peter enjoyns Subjection to, was Nero the Tyrant: And from thence you infer, that it is our Duty to submit and yield Obedience to such. But it is not certain that this Epistle was writ in Nero's Reign: 'Tis as likely to have been writ in Claudius his time. And they that are commanded to submit, were private Persons and Strangers; they were no Consuls, no Magistrates:

Senatum ipsum Romanum, cui hæc scripta sunt. Quid inde assequeris? cùm nullum præceptum cui ratio aliqua adjuncta est, quenquam ultra illam præcepti rationem obligare aut soleat aut possit. *Estote subjecti*, ὑποτάγητε, id est, si vim verbi spectes, subordinati, seu legitimè subjecti; ἡ δὲ τάξις νόμος inquit *Aristoteles*, lex est ordo. *Subjecti estote propter Dominum*. Quamobrem? quia cùm rex, tum præses constituitur à Deo ad ultionem facinorosorum, laudem benefacientium. *Quoniam ita voluntas est Dei*. Videlicet ut talibus obsequamur, quales hic describuntur; de aliis nullum hic verbum. Vides quam optimè hujus præcepti constet ratio; addit. v. 16. *ut liberi*, non ergò ut mancipia. Quid si versa vice ad crucem & perniciem bonorum, ad impunitatem & laudem & præmia facinororum regnent? an in perpetuum subjecti erimus non privati solùm, sed primores, sed magistratus omnes, ipse denique Senatus? Annon humana ordinatio dicitur? cur ergò potestas humana, ad constituendum quod hominibus bonum & salubre est, valebit, ad tollendum quod iisdem malum & exitiosum est, non valebit? Atqui rex ille, cui subjecti esse jubentur, erat Romæ eâ tempestate Nero tyrannus; ergò tyrannis etiam subjecti esse debemus. the Roman Senate itself, to whom these things are written. What do you achieve by that? Since no commandment, to which some reason is attached, is accustomed to, or can, bind anyone beyond the reason of that commandment. *Be subject*, ὑποτάγητε, that is, if you look at the force of the word, subordinated, or legitimately subject; ἡ δὲ τάξις νόμος, says Aristotle, order is law. *Be subject for the Lord’s sake*. For what reason? Because both the king and the governor are appointed by God for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good. *For such is the will of God*. Clearly that we should obey such as are described here; concerning others, there is not a word here. You see how well the reason for this commandment stands; he adds in verse 16, *as free*, therefore not as slaves. What if, on the contrary, they reign for the cross and destruction of the good, for the impunity and praise and rewards of evildoers? Shall we be subject forever, not only private citizens, but the leaders, but all the magistrates, indeed the Senate itself? Is it not called a human ordinance? Why then shall human power be valid for establishing what is good and healthy for men, but not be valid for removing what is evil and destructive to them? Yet that king, to whom they are commanded to be subject, was Nero the tyrant at that time in Rome; therefore we must be subject even to tyrannies. This suffices for the Replies to the Objections.

QUESTION 112

OF BOASTING
(In Two Articles)

We must now consider boasting and irony, which are parts of lying according to the Philosopher (Ethic. iv, 7). Under the first head, namely, boasting, there are two points of inquiry:

(1) To which virtue is it opposed?

(2) Whether it is a mortal sin?

FIRST ARTICLE [II-II, Q. 112, Art. 1]

Whether Boasting Is Opposed to the Virtue of Truth?

Objection 1: It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But it is possible to boast even without lying, as when a man makes a show of his own excellence. Thus it is written (Esther 1:3, 4) that Assuerus "made a great feast . . . that he might show the riches of the glory" and "of his kingdom, and the greatness and boasting of his power." Therefore boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.

Obj. 2: Further, boasting is reckoned by Gregory (Moral. xxiii, 4) to be one of the four species of pride, "when," to wit, "a man boasts of having what he has not." Hence it is written (Jer. 48:29, 30): "We have heard the pride of Moab, he is exceeding proud: his haughtiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the loftiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that the strength thereof is not according to it." Moreover, Gregory says (Moral. xxxi, 7) that boasting arises from vainglory. Now pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore boasting is opposed, not to truth, but to humility.

Obj. 3: Further, boasting seems to be occasioned by riches; wherefore it is written (Wis. 5:8): "What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?" Now excess of riches seems to belong to the sin of covetousness, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore boasting is not opposed to truth.

On the contrary, The Philosopher says (Ethic. ii, 7; iv, 7), that boasting is opposed to truth.

I answer that, Jactantia (boasting) seems properly to denote the uplifting of self by words: since if a man wishes to throw (jactare) a thing far away, he lifts it up high. And to uplift oneself, properly speaking, is to talk of oneself above oneself [*Or 'tall-talking' as we should say in English]. This happens in two ways. For sometimes a man speaks of himself, not above what he is in himself, but above that which he is esteemed by men to be: and this the Apostle declines to do when he says (2 Cor. 12:6): "I forbear lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or anything he heareth of me." In another way a man uplifts himself in words, by speaking of himself above that which he is in reality. And since we should judge of things as they are in themselves, rather than as others deem them to be, it follows that boasting denotes more properly the uplifting of self above what one is in oneself, than the uplifting of self above what others think of one: although in either case it may be called boasting. Hence boasting properly so called is opposed to truth by way of excess.

Reply Obj. 1: This argument takes boasting as exceeding men's opinion.

Reply Obj. 2: The sin of boasting may be considered in two ways. First, with regard to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth; as stated (in the body of the article and Q. 110, A. 2). Secondly, with regard to its cause, from which more frequently though not always it arises: and thus it proceeds from pride as its inwardly moving and impelling cause. For when a man is uplifted inwardly by arrogance, it often results that outwardly he boasts of great things about himself; though sometimes a man takes to boasting, not from arrogance, but from some kind of vanity, and delights therein, because he is a boaster by habit. Hence arrogance, which is an uplifting of self above oneself, is a kind of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is very often its cause. For this reason Gregory reckons boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, the boaster frequently aims at obtaining glory through his boasting, and so, according to Gregory, it arises from vainglory considered as its end.
[context] Reply Obj. 3: Wealth also causes boasting, in two ways.

->QUÆSTIO CXII<-

DE JACTANTIA. — In duos articulos divisa.

Postea considerandum est de jactantia — et ironia, quæ sunt partes mendacii, secundum Philosophum, in 4 Ethic., cap. 7.
Primo autem circa jactantiam quæruntur duo: 1° cui virtuti opponatur; 2° utrum sit peccatum mortale.

->ARTICULUS PRIMUS<-

Utrum jactantia opponatur virtuti veritatis.

Ad primum sic proceditur. 1. Videtur quod jactantia non opponatur virtuti veritatis. Veritati enim opponitur mendacium. Sed quandoque potest esse jactantia etiam sine mendacio; sicut cum aliquis suam excellentiam ostentat: dicitur enim Esther 1, 3: *Assuerus fecit grande convivium..., ut ostenderet divitias gloriæ suæ, ac regni sui* (1) ac magnitudinem, atque excellentiam potentiæ suæ. Ergo jactantia non opponitur virtuti veritatis.
2. Præterea, jactantia ponitur a Gregorio 23, Moral., cap. 4, a princ. una de quatuor speciebus superbiæ, cum scilicet quis jactat se habere quod non habet; unde dicitur Jerem. 48, 29: *Audivimus superbiam Moab (superbus est valde), sublimitatem ejus, et arrogantiam, et superbiam, et altitudinem cordis ejus. Ego scio, ait Dominus, jactantiam ejus et quod non sit juxta eum virtus ejus.* Et 31 Moral., cap. 7, a med., Gregorius dicit quod jactantia oriatur ex inani gloria. Superbia autem et inanis gloria opponuntur virtuti humilitatis. Ergo jactantia non opponitur veritati, sed humilitati.

<margin>ART. I. — Jactantia proprie dicta est vitium, quo quispiam exterius se effert, supra id quod in ipso est. Jactantia licet quoad vocabuli usum dicatur etiam de ostentatione veri supra opinionem seu cognitionem aliorum, ut de vitio ex suo genere (sic enim tantum proprie sumitur), non dicitur nisi de opposito veritatis, per modum excessus; quoniam sic tantum est nomen vitii ex suo genere. Ostentatio namque veri supra cognitionem aliorum, non est mala ex suo genere, sed quandoque bona juxta necessitatem aut utilitatem, quandoque mala, propter malum finem (Cajetanus).</margin>

(1) Vulgata: ... Divitias gloriæ regni sui.

<column-break/>

3. Præterea, jactantia ex divitiis causari videtur; unde dicitur Sap. 5, 8: *Quid nobis profuit superbia, aut diviliarum jactantia quid contulit nobis?* Sed superfluitas divitiarum videtur pertinere ad peccatum avaritiæ, quod opponitur justitiæ vel liberalitati. Non ergo jactantia opponitur veritati.
— Sed contra, est quod Philosophus dicit in 2 et in 4 Ethic., cap. 7, utrobique (1) jactantiam opponi veritati.

RESPONDEO dicendum quod jactantia proprie importare videtur quod homo verbis se extollat. Illa enim quæ vult homo longe jactare, in altum elevat. Tunc autem proprie aliquis se extollit, quando de se supra se aliquid dicit. Quod quidem contingit dupliciter: — quandoque enim aliquis loquitur de se, non quidem supra id quod in se est, sed supra id quod de eo homines opinantur; quod Apostolus refugiens dicit 2 ad Cor. 12, 6: *Parco, ne quis existimet me supra id quod videt in me, aut audit aliquid ex me.* — Alio modo aliquis per verba se extollit, loquens de se supra id quod in se est secundum rei veritatem. Et quia magis aliquis judicandum, secundum quod in se est, quam secundum quod est in opinione aliorum, inde est quod magis proprie dicitur jactantia, quando aliquis effert se supra id quod in ipso est quam quando effert se supra id quod est in opinione aliorum; quamvis utroque modo jactantia dici possit. Et ideo **jactantia proprie dicta opponitur veritati per modum excessus.**

Ad primum ergo dicendum quod ratio illa procedit de jactantia, secundum quod excedit opinionem.
Ad secundum dicendum quod jactantiæ peccatum considerari potest dupliciter: — uno modo secundum speciem actus, et sic opponitur veritati, ut dictum est in corp., et quæst. 110, art. 2; — alio modo secundum causam suam, ex qua etsi non semper, tamen frequentius accidit, et sic procedit quidem ex superbia sicut ex causa interiori motiva et impellente; ex hoc enim quod aliquis interius per arrogantiam supra seipsum elevatur, sequitur plerumque quod exterius majora quædam de se jactet, licet quandoque non ex arrogantia, sed ex quadam vanitate aliquis ad jactantiam procedat, et in hoc delectetur, quia talis est secundum habitum. Et ideo arrogantia, per quam aliquis supra seipsum extollitur, est species superbiæ; non tamen idem jactantiæ, sed ut frequentius ejus causa. Et propter hoc Gregorius jactantiam ponit inter superbiæ species. Tendit autem jactator plerumque ad hoc quod gloriam consequatur per suam jactantiam; et ideo secundum Gregorium ex inani gloria oritur secundum rationem finis.

(1) In Nicol. deest verbum utrobique.
