->QUESTION CXII<-

ON BOASTING. — Divided into two articles.

Next, we must consider boasting and irony, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher, in 4 *Ethics*, ch. 7.
First, regarding boasting, two points are inquired into: 1. To which virtue is it opposed; 2. Whether it is a mortal sin.

->ARTICLE FIRST<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, it is proceeded as follows. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes boasting can exist even without a lie; such as when someone shows off their own excellence: for it is said in Esther 1:3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast... that he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom* and the greatness and excellence of his power. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is placed by Gregory, 23 *Morals*, ch. 4, from the beginning, as one of the four species of pride, namely when someone boasts of having what they do not have; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that his virtue is not according to it.* And in 31 *Morals*, ch. 7, near the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from vainglory. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

ART. I. — Boasting, strictly speaking, is a vice whereby someone outwardly exalts oneself above that which is in oneself. Although boasting, according to the use of the word, may also be spoken of regarding the display of truth beyond the opinion or knowledge of others—as it is a vice from its own genus (for thus it is only strictly taken)—it is not spoken of except as the opposite of truth, by way of excess; since only then is it the name of a vice from its own genus. For the display of truth beyond the knowledge of others is not evil from its own genus, but is sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes evil, on account of an evil end (Cajetan).

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by wealth; hence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of wealth seems to pertain to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— But on the contrary, there is what the Philosopher says in 2 and 4 *Ethics*, ch. 7, in both places that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that boasting, strictly speaking, seems to imply that a man exalts himself by words. For those things that a man wishes to boast about far and wide, he elevates on high. Now, someone properly exalts oneself when they say something about themselves that is above themselves. This occurs in two ways: sometimes someone speaks of themselves not indeed above that which is in them, but above that which men opine of them; which the Apostle, avoiding, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or heareth anything of me.* — In another way, someone exalts oneself by words, speaking of oneself above that which is in oneself according to the truth of the matter. And because one is more to be judged according to what is in oneself than according to what is in the opinion of others, it is that it is more properly called boasting when someone exalts oneself above what is in oneself than when one exalts oneself above what is in the opinion of others; although in both ways it can be called boasting. And therefore **boasting, strictly speaking, is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds concerning boasting as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way, according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body [of the article], and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way, according to its cause, from which, although not always, yet more frequently it happens, and thus it indeed proceeds from pride as from an interior motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is elevated interiorly through arrogance above themselves, it follows for the most part that they outwardly boast of certain greater things about themselves, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and takes pleasure in this, because such is their habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is exalted above themselves, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is, for the most part, its cause. And for this reason, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. A boaster tends for the most part toward the end of obtaining glory through their boasting; and therefore, according to Gregory, it arises from vainglory according to the nature of the end.

This page discusses the definition and moral classification of boasting, distinguishing it as a vice of excess that is formally opposed to the virtue of truth, while noting its causal relationship to pride and vainglory.

Some are delighted in the very fiction; of which it is said in 3 Ethics, chapter 7, from the middle, that it seems more vain than evil; for the same reason applies to lying and simulation. — It may, however, happen that someone simulates the perfection of sanctity, which is not necessary for salvation; and such simulation is not always a mortal sin, nor is it always accompanied by a mortal sin.

->QUESTION CXII<-

ON BOASTING. — Divided into two articles.

Next, it should be considered about boasting — and irony, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher, in 4 Ethics, chapter 7.
First, regarding boasting, two things are asked: 1° to which virtue it is opposed; 2° whether it is a mortal sin.

->ARTICLE I<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, we proceed thus. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes boasting can occur even without lying; as when someone shows off his excellence: it is said in Esther 1, 3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast..., to show off the glory of his riches, and of his kingdom* (1) and his greatness, and his excellence of power. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is mentioned by Gregory in 23, Moral., chapter 4, as one of the four species of pride, when someone boasts of having what he does not; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48, 29: *We have heard the pride of Moab (he is very proud), his lofty place, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the height of his heart. I know, says the Lord, his boasting and that it is not according to him a virtue.* And in 31 Moral., chapter 7, from the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from empty glory. Pride and empty glory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

ART. I. — Boasting, properly speaking, is a vice by which someone shows off himself above what is in himself. Boasting may be said even of the showing off of the true above the opinion or knowledge of others, as of a vice of its own kind (for it is only properly taken in this sense), but it is not said of the opposite of truth, in the manner of excess; for it is only called a vice of its own kind in this way. The showing off of the true above the knowledge of others is not bad in itself, but sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes bad, because of a bad end (Cajetanus).

(1) Vulgata:... the glory of his kingdom.

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by wealth; hence it is said in Wisdom 5, 8: *What profit has our pride brought us, or what has the boasting of riches brought us?* But the excess of wealth seems to belong to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— On the contrary, it is said that the Philosopher says in 2 and in 4 Ethics, chapter 7, both places (1) that boasting is opposed to truth.

I answer that boasting, properly speaking, seems to mean that a man exalts himself with words. For that which a man wishes to boast about, he raises high. Then, properly speaking, a man exalts himself when he says something about himself above what is in himself. This happens in two ways: — for sometimes a man speaks of himself, not above what is in himself, but above what men think of him; which the Apostle refutes in 2 Corinthians 12, 6: *I am afraid lest anyone should think more highly of me than he sees in me or hears from me.* — In another way, a man exalts himself by words when he speaks of himself above what is in himself according to the truth of things. And because a man is more to be judged according to what is in himself than according to what others think of him, it is for this reason that boasting is more properly said when a man shows himself above what is in himself than when he shows himself above what others think of him; although boasting may be said in either way. And therefore, **boasting, properly speaking, is opposed to truth in the manner of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it should be said that this argument proceeds from boasting, in so far as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it should be said that the sin of boasting may be considered in two ways: — one way, according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body, and question 110, article 2; — another way, according to its cause, from which, although not always, it often happens, and thus it proceeds from pride, as from an inner, motive, and impelling cause; for from that which a man, inwardly, by arrogance, exalts himself above himself, it often follows that he externally boasts of greater things about himself, although sometimes he proceeds to boasting and takes delight in it from a certain vanity, because such is according to his habit. And therefore, arrogance, by which a man is exalted above himself, is a species of pride; it is not, however, the same as boasting, but rather the more frequent cause of it. And for this reason Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. The boaster usually aims at obtaining glory through his boasting; and therefore, according to Gregory, it arises from empty glory according to the reason of the end.

Pride and vain glory, however, are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

Boasting, although it may be called so regarding the use of the word even for the display of the true above the opinion or knowledge of others, as regarding a vice of its own kind (for it is only taken properly in this way), is not said except regarding the opposite of truth, in the manner of excess; since it is only a name of a vice of its own kind. I RESPOND that it must be said that boasting properly seems to import that a man extols himself with words. For that which a man wishes to boast of, he elevates far above. Now, someone properly extols himself when he says something about himself above himself. This indeed happens in two ways: — for sometimes someone speaks of himself, not indeed above what is in him, but above what men think about him; which the Apostle, fleeing, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I am sparing, lest anyone should think that I am above what he sees in me, or hears anything from me.* — In another way, someone extols himself through words, speaking of himself above what is in him according to the truth of the thing. And because someone is to be judged more according to what is in him than according to what is in the opinion of others, it is for this reason that it is more properly called boasting when someone displays himself above what is in him than when he displays himself above what is in the opinion of others; although it can be called boasting in both ways. And therefore, **boasting properly so called is opposed to truth in the manner of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that reason proceeds regarding boasting, insofar as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body, and question 110, article 2; — in another way according to its cause, from which, although not always, yet it happens more frequently, and thus it proceeds indeed from pride as from an interior motive and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is internally elevated above himself through arrogance, it usually follows that he externally boasts of certain greater things about himself, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting and takes delight in it not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, because such is his habit. And therefore, arrogance, by which someone is extolled above himself, is a species of pride; not, however, the same as boasting, but rather its more frequent cause. And for this reason, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. Now, the boaster usually tends to this, that he may attain glory through his boasting; and therefore, according to Gregory, it arises from vain glory according to the reason of the end.

THIRD ARTICLE [I, Q. 85, Art. 3]

Whether the More Universal Is First in Our Intellectual Cognition?

Objection 1: It would seem that the more universal is not first in our intellectual cognition. For what is first and more known in its own nature, is secondarily and less known in relation to ourselves. But universals come first as regards their nature, because "that is first which does not involve the existence of its correlative" (Categor. ix). Therefore the universals are secondarily known as regards our intellect.

Obj. 2: Further, the composition precedes the simple in relation to us. But universals are the more simple. Therefore they are known secondarily by us.

Obj. 3: Further, the Philosopher says (Phys. i, 1), that the object defined comes in our knowledge before the parts of its definition. But the more universal is part of the definition of the less universal, as "animal" is part of the definition of "man." Therefore the universals are secondarily known by us.

Obj. 4: Further, we know causes and principles by their effects. But universals are principles. Therefore universals are secondarily known by us.

On the contrary, "We must proceed from the universal to the singular and individual" (Phys. i, 1)

I answer that, In our knowledge there are two things to be considered. First, that intellectual knowledge in some degree arises from sensible knowledge: and, because sense has singular and individual things for its object, and intellect has the universal for its object, it follows that our knowledge of the former comes before our knowledge of the latter. Secondly, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from a state of potentiality to a state of actuality; and every power thus proceeding from potentiality to actuality comes first to an incomplete act, which is the medium between potentiality and actuality, before accomplishing the perfect act. The perfect act of the intellect is complete knowledge, when the object is distinctly and determinately known; whereas the incomplete act is imperfect knowledge, when the object is known indistinctly, and as it were confusedly. A thing thus imperfectly known, is known partly in act and partly in potentiality, and hence the Philosopher says (Phys. i, 1), that "what is manifest and certain is known to us at first confusedly; afterwards we know it by distinguishing its principles and elements." Now it is evident that to know an object that comprises many things, without proper knowledge of each thing contained in it, is to know that thing confusedly. In this way we can have knowledge not only of the universal whole, which contains parts potentially, but also of the integral whole; for each whole can be known confusedly, without its parts being known. But to know distinctly what is contained in the universal whole is to know the less common, as to "animal" indistinctly is to know it as "animal"; whereas to know "animal" distinctly is know it as "rational" or "irrational animal," that is, to know a man or a lion: therefore our intellect knows "animal" before it knows man; and the same reason holds in comparing any more universal idea with the less universal.

Moreover, as sense, like the intellect, proceeds from potentiality to act, the same order of knowledge appears in the senses. For by sense we judge of the more common before the less common, in reference both to place and time; in reference to place, when a thing is seen afar off it is seen to be a body before it is seen to be an animal; and to be an animal before it is seen to be a man, and to be a man before it seen to be Socrates or Plato; and the same is true as regards time, for a child can distinguish man from not man before he distinguishes this man from that, and therefore "children at first call men fathers, and later on distinguish each one from the others" (Phys. i, 1). The reason of this is clear: because he who knows a thing indistinctly is in a state of potentiality as regards its principle of distinction; as he who knows genus is in a state of potentiality as regards "difference." Thus it is evident that indistinct knowledge is midway between potentiality and act.

We must therefore conclude that knowledge of the singular and individual is prior, as regards us, to the knowledge of the universal; as sensible knowledge is prior to intellectual knowledge. But in both sense and intellect the knowledge of the more common precedes the knowledge of the less common.

Reply Obj. 1: The universal can be considered in two ways. First, the universal nature may be considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality--viz. the relation of one and the same to many--is due to intellectual abstraction, the universal thus considered is a secondary consideration. Hence it is said (De Anima i, 1) that the "universal animal is either nothing or something secondary." But according to Plato, who held that universals are subsistent, the universal considered thus would be prior to the particular, for the latter, according to him, are mere participations of the subsistent universals which he called ideas.

Secondly, the universal can be considered in the nature itself--for instance, animality or humanity as existing in the individual. And thus we must distinguish two orders of nature: one, by way of generation and time; and thus the imperfect and the potential come first. In this way the more common comes first in the order of nature; as appears clearly in the generation of man and animal; for "the animal is generated before man," as the Philosopher says (De Gener. Animal ii, 3). The other order is the order of perfection or of the intention of nature: for instance, act considered absolutely is naturally prior to potentiality, and the perfect to the imperfect: thus the less common comes naturally before the more common; as man comes before animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of animal but goes on to the generation of man.

Reply Obj. 2: The more common universal may be compared to the less common, as the whole, and as the part. As the whole, considering that in the more universal is potentially contained not only the less universal, but also other things, as in "animal" is contained not only "man" but also "horse." As part, considering that the less common contains in its idea not only the more common, but also more; as "man" contains not only "animal" but also "rational." Therefore "animal" in itself comes into our knowledge before "man"; but "man" comes before "animal" considered as part of the same idea.

Reply Obj. 3: A part can be known in two ways. First, absolutely considered in itself; and thus nothing prevents the parts being known before the whole, as stones are known before a house is known. Secondly as belonging to a certain whole; and thus we must needs know the whole before its parts. For we know a house vaguely before we know its different parts. So likewise principles of definition are known before the thing defined is known; otherwise the thing defined would not be known at all. But as parts
[context] of the definition they are known after. For we know man vaguely as man before we know how to distinguish all that belongs to human nature.

Tertius ar. utrum magis uniuersalia sint priora in nostra cognitione intellectuali.

Dtertium sic, proceditur. Ut quod magis uniuersalia non sint priora in nostra cognitione in-tellectuali: quia ea que sunt priora notiora secundum naturam sunt posteriora et minus nota secundum nos, sed uniuersalia sunt priora secundum naturam nostri intellectus. Preterea composita sunt priora quo ad nos et simplicia. sed uniuersalia sunt priora cioza: sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Preterea philosophus dicit in primo physicorum diffinitus prius cadit in cognitione nostra et partes diffinitionis minus uniuersali: sicut animal est pars diffinitionis hominis: et uniuersalia sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Preterea effectus euenimus et casu et principia. sed uniuersalia sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Sed si est quod or in in primo physicorum ex libris in singularia os deuenire. Respondeo dicendum quod in cognitione nostri intellectus duo os considerare. primo quidem quod cognitio intellectiua aliquo modo a sensitiua primordium sumit. et quia sensus est singularium in intellectus et uniuersalius: necesse est quod cognitio singularium quo ad nos sit uniuersalius cognitio. secundo os considerare quod intellectus nr de potentia ad actum procedit. et quod procedit de potentia in actum prius peruenit ad actum incompletum qui est medius inter potentia et actus et actus perfectus. aut perfectus ad quem peruenit intellectus est scia completa per quas distincte et determinate res cognoscuntur: actus et incompletus est scia imperfecta per quam sciuntur res indistincte sub quadaz confusione. quod enim sic cognoscitur tam quod cognoscitur in actu et quodammodo in potentia. ut in primo physicorum dicit in primo physicorum: sit primum nobis manifesta et certa confusa magis. posterius autem cognoscimus distinguendo distincte principia et elementa. manifestum est autem quod cognoscere aliquid in quo plura continentur sine hoc quod habeatur propria notitia uniuscuiusque eorum que continentur in illo est cognoscere aliquid sub confusione quadam. sic autem potest cognosci tam totum uel in quo partes continentur in potentia et totum integrale: utrumque enim totum potest cognosci in quadam confusione sine hoc quod partes distincte cognoscantur. cognoscere autem distincte id quod continetur in toto uel est habere cognitionem de re minus communi: sicut cognoscere animal indistincte et cognoscere animal in quo cum est rationale aut irrationale quod est cognoscere homine ut leonem. prius igitur occurrit intellectui nostro cognoscere animal et cognoscere homine. et cadere rone si comparem quodcumque magis uel ad minus ut sensus exit de potentia in actu sic intellectus: id et ordo

It is proceeded thus that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior according to nature are posterior and less known according to us, but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior regarding us and simple ones posterior, but universals are prior to things; thus they are known later regarding us. Furthermore, the philosopher says in the first Physicorum that the defined falls first into our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later regarding us. Furthermore, effects occur by chance and from principles, but universals are known later regarding us. But if it is as the Philosopher says in the first Physicorum, one must arrive from books to singulars. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive [cognition]. And because sense is of singulars, and intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, one must consider that our intellect proceeds from potentiality to act. And what proceeds from potentiality into act first arrives at an incomplete act, which is between potentiality and completed act. And the perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, by which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, by which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as if in act and in a certain way in potentiality. As he says in the first Physicorum, those things are first manifest and certain to us which are more confused, but we know [the] principles and elements later by distinguishing them distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of the things contained in it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, however, it is possible to know the whole, or that in which parts are contained in potentiality, and the integral whole; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of the less common thing, such as knowing "animal" indistinctly and knowing the animal in which is contained "rational" or "irrational," which is knowing "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and [then] to know "man." And if I compare any thing, whether more or less [universal], as sense goes from potentiality into act, so does the intellect; this is the order.

The order of cognition appears in sense. For more and in sense one distinguishes more, and when [something] less is known, it is more remote through [the process] of existing as a body, and [the process] of existing as a living thing; and more [is known] to exist as a living thing and to be something and to be a body, and prior to be a body and to be a substance. Or it pleases and is evident that a child from the beginning distinguishes a body and [what is] not a body; and children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, he terminates each one, as the Philosopher says in the first Physicorum book, [that] they are manifest, and he who knows something indistinctly still knows it in potentiality, or he knows it as a fiction and a principle; thus he knows them and is able to know them [distinctly]. And so, by itself, indistinct cognition is intermediate between potentiality and act. And the cognition of singulars is prior regarding us, and universal cognition is [after] sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If [one considers] both sense and intellect, the cognition of the more [universal] is prior to the cognition of the lesser and the common. To the first, it must be said that through a double [way] it can be considered. One is that through which it is considered thus, [regarding] the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true [are] the same, it has a relationship to many things. It arrives at the abstraction of the intellect; this is the end, while truly it is posterior. In the first De Anima, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior, but he placed universals as substances, and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal subsisting [things] which are called "Ideas." In another way, it can be considered with regard to the nature itself of animality or humanity as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potentiality are prior. And in this way the more [universal] is prior, which appears manifest in the generation of man and animal. For first the animal is generated, then man, as the Philosopher says in the book De Generatione Animalium. Another is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior to potentiality in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is being made; and in this way the less [universal] is prior in nature, for man is [more perfect than] animal. Nature’s intention does not rest in the generation of an animal, but it intends to generate a man. To the second, [the argument about] the more universal compared to the less universal is a whole, and through the whole it is made more universal, not only by [being] in man, but also in the horse; as it is possible that the less [universal] is contained in the future not only in the more [universal] but in others, as man [is] not only animal but rational. Thus, therefore, animal considered in itself is prior in our cognition, and man [is posterior]. If man is prior in our cognition, then animal [is known] through the reason of it. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing [is known] as [a whole] house. In another way, when it is [known] as parts of this whole and stones, it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we first know the house in a certain confusion. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining [concept] to be considered absolutely is made prior to us and defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through them, but rather those which are parts.

Furthermore, the philosopher says in the first book of physics that the first thing to fall into our cognition is the definition, and the parts of the definition are less universal. For example, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man." And universal things are later known by us. Furthermore, effects occur by chance and principles. I answer that in our intellect's cognition, two things are considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way begins from sensory cognition. And because the senses are of singular things in the intellect and more universal, it is necessary that the cognition of singular things be more universal with regard to us. Second, we consider that the intellect proceeds from potentiality to actuality. And that it proceeds from potentiality to actuality, it first arrives at an incomplete actuality, which is the middle between potentiality and actuality and the perfect actuality. The perfect actuality to which the intellect arrives is the complete knowledge by which things are known distinctly and determinately. The incomplete actuality is the imperfect knowledge by which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For this reason, things are known both in actuality and in a way in potentiality. As the first book of physics says: the first thing is manifest and certain to us, but more confused. Later, we know by distinguishing distinct principles and elements. Thirdly, whether universals are more prior in our intellectual cognition.

The third is answered thus: That universals are not more prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior are more known according to nature, but are posterior and less known according to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composites are prior to us than simples, but universals are prior to us, because they are posterior in knowledge according to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher says in the first book of the Physics that the definition falls into our cognition first, and the parts of the definition are less universal, such as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are posterior in knowledge according to us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects both by chance and by principles, but universals are posterior in knowledge according to us. But if it is asked in the first book of the Physics, from the books on singular things, how one arrives at universals, I answer that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual cognition takes its beginning in some way from sensitive cognition, and because sense is of singular things in the intellect and more universal, it is necessary that the cognition of singular things according to us be more universal than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that the intellect proceeds from potentiality to act, and that it proceeds from potentiality into act, it arrives first at an incomplete act, which is the medium between potentiality and act and the perfect act. Or the perfect act to which the intellect arrives is the complete science by which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is the imperfect science by which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potentiality, as in the first book of the Physics, it says: "Let the first be manifest and certain, and the latter we know by distinguishing the distinct principles and elements." It is manifest, however, that to know something in which several things are contained, without this that one has a proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. Thus, however, it can be known both the whole in which the parts are contained in potentiality and the integral whole; for both the whole can be known in a certain confusion without this that the parts are known distinctly. To know, however, distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing, such as to know "animal" indistinctly and to know "animal" in which it is rational or irrational, which is to know man as a lion. For more and less is known in the sense, and in the remote, by the operation of being a body, and the operation of being an animal, and more is operated upon being an animal, and the operation of being a body, and the prior is a body and a soul. [context] This," he said, "the gods enjoin; and we have already shown how they admonish the soul to turn
to God, and command it to worship Him. But the ignorant and the ungodly, who are not destined to receive favours from the gods, nor to know the immortal Jupiter, not listening to the gods and their messages, have turned away from all gods, and have not only refused to hate, but have venerated the prohibited demons. Professing to worship God, they refuse to do those things by which alone God is worshipped. For God, indeed, being the Father of all, is in need of nothing; but for us it is good to adore Him by means of justice, chastity, and other virtues, and thus to make life itself a prayer to Him, by inquiring into and imitating His nature. For inquiry," says he, "purifies and imitation deifies us, by moving us nearer to Him." He is right in so far as he proclaims God the Father, and the conduct by which we should worship Him. Of such precepts the prophetic books of the Hebrews are full, when they praise or blame the life of the saints. But in speaking of the Christians he is in error, and calumniates them as much as is desired by the demons whom he takes for gods, as if it were difficult for any man to recollect the disgraceful and shameful actions which used to be done in the theatres and temples to please the gods, and to compare with these things what is heard in our churches, and what is offered to the true God, and from this comparison to conclude where character is edified, and where it is ruined. But who but a diabolical spirit has told or suggested to this man so manifest and vain a lie, as that the Christians reverenced rather than hated the demons, whose worship the Hebrews prohibited? But that God, whom the Hebrew sages worshipped, forbids sacrifice to be offered even to the holy angels of heaven and divine powers, whom we, in this our pilgrimage, venerate and love as our most blessed fellow-citizens. For in the law which God gave to His Hebrew people He utters this menace, as in a voice of thunder: "He that sacrificeth unto any god, save unto the Lord only, he shall be utterly destroyed."[659] And that no one might suppose that this prohibition extends only to the very wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom this philosopher calls very small and inferior,--for even these are in the Scripture called gods, not of the Hebrews, but of the nations, as the Septuagint translators have shown in the psalm where it is said, "For all the gods of the nations are demons,"--that no one might suppose, I say, that sacrifice to these demons was prohibited, but that sacrifice might be offered to all or some of the celestials, it was immediately added, "save unto the Lord alone." [note 661: Augustine here warns his readers against a possible misunderstanding of the Latin word for "alone" (soli), which might be rendered "the sun."] The God of the Hebrews, then, to whom this renowned philosopher bears this signal testimony, gave to His Hebrew people a law, composed in the Hebrew language, and not obscure and unknown, but published now in every nation, and in this law it is written, "He that sacrificeth unto any god, save unto the Lord alone, he shall be utterly destroyed." What need is there to seek further proofs in the law or the prophets of this same thing? Seek, we need not say, for the passages are neither few nor difficult to find; but what need to collect and apply to my argument the proofs which are thickly sown and obvious, and by which it appears clear as day that sacrifice may be paid to none but the supreme and true God? Here is one brief but decided, even menacing, and certainly true utterance of that God whom the wisest of our adversaries so highly extol. Let this be listened to, feared, fulfilled, that there may be no disobedient soul cut off. "He that sacrifices," He says, not because He needs anything, but because it behoves us to be His possession. Hence the Psalmist in the Hebrew Scriptures sings, "I have said to the Lord, Thou art my God, for Thou needest not my good." For we ourselves, who are His own city, are His most noble and worthy sacrifice, and it is this mystery we celebrate in our sacrifices, which are well known to the faithful, as we have explained in the preceding books. For through the prophets the oracles of God declared that the sacrifices which the Jews offered as a shadow of that which was to be would cease, and that the nations, from the rising to the setting of the sun, would offer one sacrifice.
[context] From these oracles, which we now see accomplished, we have made such selections as seemed suitable to our purpose in this work.

But the unlearned and the philosophers themselves, who do not truly proceed from the Lord to obtain his gifts, and do not have the knowledge of the immortal Jupiter, not listening to both the gods and the divine men, have indeed rejected all the gods. Yet, they have chosen not only not to hate the forbidden demons, but even to revere them. Pretending to worship God, they do not do the only things through which God is adored. For God, as the father of all, needs nothing; but it is good for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very lives a path to him through imitation and instruction from him. For instruction purges the mind, while imitation deifies the affection for him by working. He preached well indeed about God the Father and told with what morals he should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrei are full of these precepts, when the life of the holy ones is either praised or blamed. But it was only among the Christians, or [these philosophers] calumniate them as much as the demons they fancy to be gods desire; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in theaters and temples regarding the service of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God, and from this to understand where there is the building up and where the ruin of morals. But who said this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fitting lie, that Christians would rather revere than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we, in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love as the most blessed citizens, the celestial holy angels and the powers of God, forbids that sacrifice be offered to anyone in his law which he gave to his people, the Hebrews; and he thundered very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And so that no one would think that it was not forbidden to sacrifice to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom he calls mimes or lesser [gods]—who were also called gods in the holy scriptures, not by the Hebrews

but by the Gentiles—which the seventy interpreters clearly placed in the psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons." Therefore, lest anyone think that sacrifice was indeed forbidden to these demons, but permitted to be offered to the celestial ones, either to all or to some, he immediately added: "unless to the Lord only," that is, unless to the Lord alone. Lest perhaps anyone, because he says "to the Lord only," might believe that God is the only one to whom he thinks he must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood that way is most easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives so great a testimony, gave a law to his own Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but now spread among all the nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of his and in his prophets to search much about this matter? Or rather, not to search, for they are not hidden or erased, but clear and frequent to collect, and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that he wished the true and highest God to be sacrificed to no one at all except to himself. Behold, this one thing, briefly or rather weightily, menacingly, but truthfully said by that God whom their most learned men preach as so excellent: let it be heard, feared, and fulfilled, lest the destruction follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," he says, "shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord only." Not because he needs any thing, but because it is expedient for us that we should be his. For to him it is sung in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, you are my God, for you do not need my goods." And the most excellent and best sacrifice of him is we ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our oblations, which are known to the faithful, as we disputed in the preceding books. For the prophets of the Hebrews interpreted through oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future were to cease, and that one sacrifice would be offered by the Gentiles from the rising of the sun even to its setting, as we now see being done.

Augustine refutes the claim that Christians irrationally hate demons, arguing that the Hebrew law explicitly prohibits the worship of such spirits. He asserts that the one true God demands exclusive sacrifice, a tradition now fulfilled by the universal Christian sacrifice, replacing the temporary rituals of the Old Testament.

The gods are mocked and the idol is worshipped everywhere.
The wise man and nature itself: for whom the fate of the world has not yet come to pass, and who have not yet received the gifts of the day: let no one have the knowledge of the immortal Jupiter: you will not hear of the gods and divine men: the gods have indeed withdrawn from you: the demons, not even with the hatred of any, have been chosen by you to be worshipped. The gods, however, are imitated by those who worship them alone, for the god is not worshipped by them. Indeed, no one can be satisfied with the god alone: but for us, it is the justice and chastity and other virtues that are to be worshipped: we should make our lives in imitation and instruction of him. The instruction purges the mind, and the imitation elevates the affection toward him through action. Well, he has indeed spoken of the god and said where the worship of the god should be. The prophetic books are full of these things, the Hebrews: whether they praise or condemn the holy life. But for the Christians, it was otherwise: they were either accused of being so wicked that the demons, whom they thought were gods, would have it that it is difficult for anyone to recall the shameful and disgraceful acts of worship toward the gods, which were performed in the theaters and temples, and which were read, spoken, and heard in the churches: or that the god would have it that one should offer something to him: from this it is clear where the building and where the ruin of the world is. Who has said this to this man, unless it is the devil's spirit, which is empty and deceitful: which the demons, who are thought to be gods, would rather honor than hate the Christians? But the god whom you worship is wise, the Hebrews, and the celestial and holy angels, and the virtues of God, whom the most blessed men, the citizens of this strange pilgrimage of mortal life, honor and love: it is forbidden to sacrifice to idols in the law which he gave to his people, the Hebrews: and he very strongly says, "You shall not sacrifice to idols." And so that no one might think that the worst earthly spirits, whom he calls minor demons, should be sacrificed to: nor should you offer sacrifices to them, for they are themselves called gods in the holy scriptures: not the Hebrews.

But to the Gentiles: for this is what the seventy interpreters of the psalm have said. For the gods of the Gentiles are demons: so that no one might think that these demons are to be sacrificed to: nor that the celestial or other spirits, or some others, should be sacrificed to: he then added: unless to the one God: unless to the Lord alone: lest someone might say, "To the one God," and think that he is the one to whom sacrifices are to be made. This is clearly understood from the Greek scriptures. The God, therefore, to the Hebrews, who is so great and mighty, has given testimony: he gave his law to his people, the Hebrews: he has written it in the Hebrews, not obscurely or unknown: but it is known to all, and is spoken of in the law. "You shall not sacrifice to idols," unless to the one God. What need is there for anyone to inquire into this law or into the prophets about this matter? Rather, do not inquire: it is not obscure or hidden: but it is suitable and frequent: and in this discussion I place before you what will make it clearer: that no one should sacrifice to any other god except himself, and to the highest. Behold, this is one thing briefly, mildly, and seriously said: it is spoken by that god who is most wise and learned: listen: fear: fulfill: lest the punishment of destruction befall the disobedient. "You shall not sacrifice to idols," unless to the one God. It is not because of the need of the thing, but because it is expedient for us to be part of it. To this, he says in the sacred Hebrew writings: "I have said, 'The Lord is my God,' for I have need of good things." This man, however, is the most excellent and best sacrifice himself. This is the city of his: whose mystery is celebrated with offerings, which are known to the faithful: as I have disputed in the previous books. He has ceased to offer the victims which the shadow of the future offered to the Jews: and one sacrifice, the Gentiles from the rising of the sun to its setting, as I see, is offered to the prophets, the Hebrews, by the oracles.

...warn the gods and worship Him everywhere. But the learned and the nature itself, to whom the true fate has not proceeded from the Lord to obtain gifts, not having the notion of the immortal Jupiter, do not hear the gods and divine men. They have indeed receded from all gods, but they have chosen to revere the forbidden demons, not only with hatred, but also with reverence. Those who simulate themselves as worshipping God do not act according to the only thing by which God is adored. For God, as He is equal to all, needs nothing, but it is well for us to adore Him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making Him Himself the very life through imitation and instruction concerning Him. For instruction purifies, and imitation deifies the affection toward Him in working. He indeed preached well of God and said in what manner He is to be worshipped. By these precepts, the prophetic books of the Hebrews are full, whether they praise or blame the holy life. But in the Christians, it was only that the demons, whom he thinks are gods, slander as much as they wish, as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in the theaters and temples for the worship of the gods, and which are read, said, or heard in the churches, or what is offered to God. And from this, one may understand where the building and where the ruin of morals is. Who, however, said or inspired this to him, unless it was the diabolical spirit, so vain and apt a lie, that the Christians revere the forbidden demons worshipped by the Hebrews rather than hate them? But that God whom the wise Hebrews worshipped, and the celestial saints, and the virtues of God whom we have venerated and loved as the most blessed citizens in this mortal pilgrimage, forbids to be sacrificed, as He said in His law which He gave to His people the Hebrews, and He added very clearly, saying: "He who sacrifices to the gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone should think that the command to sacrifice was given to the worst and earthly spirits, whom he calls mimoi or minors, because the demons themselves are called gods in the Holy Scriptures, not the Hebrews

but the Gentiles, which the seventy interpreters of the Psalm placed, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons." Lest anyone should think that it was forbidden to these demons, but permitted to the celestial ones, or to all, or to some, he soon added: "except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only, lest perhaps anyone should think that "to the Lord alone" means that God is the only one to whom one should sacrifice. This is not to be understood so in the Greek Scriptures, which is easily found. Therefore, God, to whom the Hebrews gave such great testimony, gave His law to His people the Hebrews, written in Hebrew, not obscure or unknown, but already diffamed among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to the gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there to inquire much in this law of His and His prophets about this matter? Indeed, not to inquire. For they are not obscure or rare, but apt and frequent, and in this dispute of mine, to place those things by which it appears more clearly that no one except God alone and the highest wished to be sacrificed. Behold, this one thing, briefly, or rather greatly, threateningly, but truthfully, said by that God whom the most learned of the Hebrews preach as so excellent: "Let them hear, let them fear, let them fulfill, lest the unobedient be rooted out." "He who sacrifices to the gods shall be rooted out," he says, "except to the Lord only." Not because it is necessary for someone, but because it is expedient for us that we be His things. For to this one, the Hebrews say in the sacred letters: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for I have need of no good things of mine." But we ourselves are the most excellent and best sacrifice of this one. This is His city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we disputed in the preceding books. The Hebrews prophetic oracles interjected that the sacrifices which the Jews were offering in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to the setting would offer one sacrifice, as we see it already happening, through the prophets.

[context] Menstruation is promoted by using hare's gall,
in unwashed wool, as a pessary: Olympias of Thebe adds hyssop and nitre. Ashes, too, of deer's horns are taken in drink for the same purpose, and for derangements of the uterus they are applied topically, as also bull's gall, used as a pessary with opium, in the proportion of two oboli. It is a good plan, too, to use fumigations for the uterus, made with deer's hair, burnt. Hinds, they say, when they find themselves pregnant, are in the habit of swallowing a small stone. This stone, when found in their excrements, or in the uterus—for it is to be found there as well—attached to the body as an amulet, is a preventive of abortion. There are also certain small stones, found in the heart and uterus of these animals, which are very useful for women during pregnancy and in travail. As to the kind of pumice-stone which is similarly found in the uterus of the cow, we have already mentioned it when treating of the formation of that animal. A wolf's fat, applied externally, acts emolliently upon the uterus, and the liver of a wolf is very soothing for pains in that organ. It is found advantageous for women, when near delivery, to eat wolf's flesh, or, if they are in travail, to have a person near them who has eaten it; so much so, indeed, that it will act as a countercharm even to any noxious spells which may have been laid upon them. In case, however, a person who has eaten wolf's flesh should happen to enter the room at the moment of parturition, dangerous effects will be sure to follow. The hare, too, is remarkably useful for the complaints of females: the lights of that animal, dried and taken in drink, are beneficial to the uterus; the liver, taken in water with Samian earth, acts as an emmenagogue; and the rennet brings away the after-birth, due care being taken by the patient not to bathe the day before. Applied in wool as a pessary, with saffron and leek-juice, this last acts as an expellent upon the dead fœtus. It is a general opinion that the uterus of a hare, taken with the food, promotes the conception of male offspring, and that a similar effect is produced by using the testes and rennet of that animal. It is thought, too, that a leveret, taken from the uterus of its dam, is a restorative of fruitfulness to women who are otherwise past child-bearing. But it is the blood of a hare's fœtus that the magicians recommend males to drink: while for young girls they prescribe nine pellets of hare's dung, to ensure a durable firmness to the breasts. For a similar purpose, also, they apply hare's rennet with honey; and to prevent hairs from growing again when once removed, they use a liniment of hare's blood. For inflations of the uterus, it is found a good plan to apply wild boars' dung or swine's dung topically with oil: but a still more effectual remedy is to dry the dung, and sprinkle it, powdered, in the patient's drink, even though she should be in a state of pregnancy or suffering the pains of child-birth. By administering sow's milk with honied wine, parturition is facilitated; and if taken by itself it will promote the secretion of the milk when deficient in nursing women. By rubbing the breasts of females with sow's blood they are prevented from becoming too large. If pains are felt in the breasts, they will be alleviated by drinking asses' milk; and the same milk, taken with honey, has considerable efficacy as an emmenagogue. Stale fat, too, from the same animal, heals ulcerations of the uterus: applied as a pessary, in wool, it acts emolliently upon indurations of that organ; and, applied fresh by itself, or in water when stale, it has all the virtues of a depilatory. An ass's milt, dried and applied in water to the breasts, promotes the secretion of the milk; and used in the form of a fumigation, it acts as a corrective upon the uterus. A fumigation made with a burnt ass's hoof; placed beneath a woman, accelerates parturition, so much so, indeed, as to expel the dead fœtus even: hence it is that it should only be employed in cases of miscarriage, it having a fatal effect upon the living fœtus. Asses' dung, applied fresh, has a wonderful effect, they say, in arresting discharges of blood in females: the same, too, with the ashes of this dung, which, used as a pessary, are very good for the uterus. If the skin is rubbed with the foam from a horse's mouth for forty days together, before the first hair has made its appearance, it will effectually prevent the growth thereof: a decoction, too, made from deer's antlers is productive of a similar effect, being all the better if they are used quite fresh. Mares' milk, used as an injection, is highly beneficial to the uterus. Where the fœtus is felt to be dead in the uterus, the lichens or excrescences from a horse's legs, taken in fresh water, will act as an expellent: an effect produced also by a fumigation made with the hoofs or dry dung of that animal. Procidence of the uterus is arrested by using butter, in the form of an injection; and indurations of that organ are removed by similarly employing ox-gall, with oil of roses, turpentine being applied externally in wool. They say, too, that a fumigation, made from ox-dung, acts as a corrective upon procidence of the uterus, and facilitates parturition; and that conception is promoted by the use of cows' milk. It is a well-known fact that sterility is often entailed by suffering in child-birth; an evil which may be averted, Olympias of Thebes assures us, by rubbing the parts, before sexual intercourse, with bull's gall, serpents' fat, verdigrease, and honey. In cases, too, where menstruation is too abundant, the external parts should be sprinkled with a solution of calf's gall, the moment before the sexual congress; a method which acts emolliently also upon indurations of the abdomen. Applied to the navel as a liniment, it arrests excessive discharges, and is generally beneficial to the uterus. The proportions generally adopted are—one denarius of gall, one-third of a denarius of opium, and as much oil of almonds as may appear to be requisite; the whole being applied in sheep's wool. The gall, too, of a bull-calf is beaten up with half the quantity of honey, and kept in readiness for the treatment of uterine diseases. If a woman about the time of conception eats roasted veal with the plant aristolochia, she will bring forth a male child, we are assured. Calf's marrow, boiled in wine and water with the suet, and applied as a pessary, is good for ulcerations of the uterus; the same, too, with foxes' fat and cats' dung, the last being applied with resin and oil of roses. It is considered a remarkably good plan to subject the uterus to fumigations made with burnt goats' horns. The blood of the wild goat, mixed with sea-palm, acts as a depilatory. The gall of the other kinds of goat, used as an injection, acts emolliently upon callosities of the uterus, and ensures conception immediately after menstruation: it possesses also the virtues of a depilatory, the application being left for three days upon the flesh after the hair has been removed. The midwives assure us that she-goats' urine, taken in drink, and the dung, applied topically, will arrest uterine discharges, however much in excess. The membrane in which the kid is enclosed in the uterus, dried and taken in wine, acts as an expellent upon the after-birth. For affections of the uterus, it is thought a desirable plan to fumigate it with burnt kids' hair; and for discharges of blood, kids' rennet is administered in drink, or seed of henbane is applied. According to Osthanes, if a woman's loins are rubbed with blood taken from the ticks upon a black wild bull, she will be inspired with an aversion to sexual intercourse: she will forget, too, her former love, by taking a he-goat's urine in drink, some nard being mixed with it to disguise the loathsome taste.

For infants there is nothing more useful than butter, either by itself or in combination with honey; for dentition more particularly, for soreness of the gums, and for ulcerations of the mouth. A wolf's tooth, attached to the body, prevents infants from being startled, and acts as a preservative against the maladies attendant upon dentition; an effect equally produced by making use of a wolf's skin. The larger teeth, also, of a wolf, attached to a horse's neck, will render him proof against all weariness, it is said. A hare's rennet, applied to the breasts of the nurse, effectually prevents diarrhœa in the infant suckled by her. An ass's liver, mixed with a little panax, and dropped into the mouth of an infant, will preserve it from epilepsy and other diseases to which infants are liable; this, however, must be done for forty days, they say. An ass's skin, too, thrown over infants, renders them insensible to fear. The first teeth shed by a horse, attached as an amulet to infants, facilitate dentition, and are better still, when not allowed to touch the ground. For pains in the spleen, an ox's milt is administered in honey, and applied topically; and for running ulcers it is used as an application, with honey. A calf's milt, boiled in wine, is beaten up, and applied to incipient ulcers of the mouth. The magicians take the brains of a she-goat, and, after passing them through a gold ring, drop them into the mouth of the infant before it takes the breast, as a preservative against epilepsy and other infantile diseases. Goats' dung, attached to infants in a piece of cloth, prevents them from being restless, female infants in particular. By rubbing the gums of infants with goats' milk or hare's brains, dentition is greatly facilitated.

Cato was of opinion that hare's flesh, taken as a diet, is provocative of sleep. It is a vulgar notion, too, that this diet confers beauty for nine days on those who use it; a silly play upon words, no doubt, but a notion which has gained far too extensively not to have had some real foundation. According to the magicians, the gall of a she-goat, but only of one that has been sacrificed, applied to the eyes or placed beneath the pillow, has a narcotic effect. Too profuse perspiration is checked by rubbing the body with ashes of burnt goats' horns mixed with oil of myrtle.

Among the aphrodisiacs, we find mentioned, a wild boar's gall, applied externally; swine's marrow, taken inwardly; asses' fat, mixed with the grease of a gander and applied as a liniment; the virulent substance described by Virgil as distilling from mares when covered;
[context] and the dried testes of a horse, pulverized and mixed with the drink.

the suds of soap applied to it. Olympias of Thebes added hyssop and nitre. Drink the ash of stag's horn. It is also good for a struggling womb. Also, apply it as a plaster, and apply bull's bile with two obols of opium. It is beneficial to fumigate the womb with stag hair. They relate that does, when they feel they are pregnant, swallow a small stone, which the owner keeps, once found in the excrement or in the womb (for it is found there too), and ties to the body. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb, very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. For the pumice stone, which is found in the uterus of cows in a similar way, we spoke of in the nature of cattle. Wolf fat applied softens the womb. It also prevails against the harmful effects of plasters applied to its pains. And it is not beneficial. Or if they are beginning to go into labor, it should be near what she has eaten. To the point that it prevails even against harmful applied plasters. And it is indeed a small thing to supervene. The use of the hare is great for women. Dried lung, drunk, aids the womb. For hemorrhages, drink the liver with Samian earth in water. For the afterbirth, rennet. They avoid daily baths. Also, when applied with saffron and leek juice, and inserted in wool, it expels dead fetuses. If the wombs of hares are eaten, they believe that males are conceived. They think this is also achieved by their testicles and rennet. That the conception of a hare, taken from the uterus, brings back fertility to those who have ceased to bear children. But the conception of a hare is also healthy, and the Magi give it to a man to drink. Likewise, nine grains of dung to a virgin, so that her breasts may stand perpetually. Also with rennet. For that reason, when mixed with honey, it is applied to the blood when they do not want pulled-out hairs to grow back again. For the inflation of the womb, it is beneficial to apply boar or pig dung with oil. It is more effective to stop it if the flour is dry or sprinkled into a drink, as if it torments a pregnant woman or a woman in labor. Swine's milk drunk with honeyed wine aids the labor of women. But drunk by itself, it replenishes the failing breasts of women who have given birth. The same, smeared with the blood of a female pig, causes them to grow less. If they ache, soothe them with the drinking of ass's milk. Which, taken with added honey, also aids their purgations. The old suet of the same animal heals ulcerations of the womb: and when applied in wool, it softens the hardness of the womb. But when applied fresh or old with water, it holds the power of a psilothrum. The old spleen of the same animal, applied with water, makes breasts abundant. It clears the face. Fumigated ass's hooves hasten labor, so that it may even call forth an abortion; nor is it applied otherwise than that it kills the living fetus. If the fresh dung of the same animal is applied, it is said to stop hemorrhages of blood miraculously. And also the ash of the same dung, which is also beneficial to the womb when applied. Mare's foam, applied for forty days before they are born, stops the first hairs. Likewise, stag's horn is learned. Or if the horns are fresh. Wombs are aided by being washed with mare's milk. But if the labor feels dead, the spleen drunk in sweet water expels it. Likewise, fumigation with hooves or dry dung. It checks drooping faces when infused with butter. Bull's bile, mixed with rose oil, opens a hardened womb, applied externally in wool with turpentine resin. They also say that by fumigating with dung from a bull, drooping wombs are restrained and labor is aided. But conception [is aided] by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that sterility occurs because of the vexation of labor. Olympias of Thebes affirms that this is corrected with bull's bile and the fat of serpents and verdigris, with honey added to the medicated parts before intercourse. They also promise that if they eat calf's meat roasted with birthwort around the time of conception, they will give birth to males. Calf marrow, boiled in wine and water with suet, is beneficial for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise, fox fat, and cat excrement applied with resin and rose oil. They think it most useful to fumigate the womb with goat horn. The blood of wild goats with sea palm pulls out hairs. But the bile of the others, when sprinkled, softens the calluses of the womb and makes conception possible after purgation. Thus also the power of the psilothrum is effected; it is kept applied for three days after the hairs are pulled out. Midwives promise that an immense hemorrhage is stopped if goat urine is drunk, and if the dung is applied. The membrane of goats, boiled in water and taken old in a drink in wine, expels the afterbirth. They think it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a hemorrhage of blood, to drink rennet or apply henbane seed. If the loins of a black wild bull are pricked with goat blood, it is said that a weariness of sex is caused in the woman, says Aeschines. The same, goat urine drunk as a love potion, mixed with spikenard because of the aroma. For infants, nothing is more useful than butter, by itself and with honey, both privately in teething, and for the gums, and for sores of the mouth. A wolf's tooth tied to an infant prevents terrors and the diseases of teething. Which also the wolf's skin provides. Indeed, their largest teeth, when tied to horses, are said to provide an indefatigable speed. The belly of infants is stopped by rabbit rennet applied to the breast. Ass's liver, instilled into the mouth with a little all-heal mixed in, protects infants from epileptic diseases and others. They instruct that this be done for forty days. And ass's skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that first fall from horses provide easy teething for infants when tied to them. More effectively if they have not touched the ground. Calf's spleen should be eaten in honey. And applied for pain of the spleen. For flowing ulcers with honey. Calf's spleen boiled in wine and crushed and applied [cures] small ulcers of the mouth. Goat brain, passed through a gold ring before milk is given to infants, should be instilled against epilepsy and other diseases of infants. Goat dung tied in a cloth restrains restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat's milk or hare's brain make teething easy. Cato thinks that sleep is induced if hare is taken in food. The common people also think it gives grace to the body for nine days in the same place. To which, however, some cause must underlie such a great persuasion. The Magi say that sleep is induced if the bile of a sacrificed goat is applied only to the eyes or placed under the pillow. Ash of goat horn, smeared with myrtle oil, inhibits sweats. But boar's bile, applied, stimulates intercourse. Likewise, swine marrow drunk. Ass's suet mixed with the fat of a male goose, applied. Likewise from the intercourse of horses, according to Virgil

[margin] Solutions of the Arguments.
For the first, it is clear that there is no doubt but that, just as, with God's permission, they can kill men, so also can devils taken off that member, as well as others, truly and actually. But then the devils do not work through the medium of witches, concerning which mention has already been made. And from this the answer to the second argument is also made clear. But this is to be said: that God allows more power of witchcraft over the genital forces because, etc.; and therefore even allows that that member should be truly and actually taken off. But it is not valid to say that this always happens. For it would not be after the manner of witchcraft for it to happen so; and even the witches, when they do such works, do not pretend that they have not the power to restore the member when they wish to and know how to do so. From which it is clear that it is not actually taken off, but only by a glamour. As for the third, concerning the metamorphosis of Lot's wife, we say that this was actual, and not a glamour. And as to the fourth, that devils can create certain substantial shapes, and therefore can also remove them: it is to be said with regard to Pharaoh's magicians that they made true serpents; and that devils can, with the help of another agent, produce certain effects on imperfect creatures which they cannot on men, who are God's chief care. For it is said: Does God care for oxen? They can, nevertheless, with the permission of God, do to men true and actual harm, as also they can create a glamour of harm, and by this the answer to the last argument is made clear.

[margin] PART I. QUESTION X. Whether Witches can by some Glamour Change Men into Beasts.
Here we declare the truth as to whether and how witches transform men into beasts. And it is argued that this is not possible, from the following passage of Episcopus (XXVI, 5): Whoever believes that it is possible for any creature to be changed for the better or for the worse, or to be transformed into any other shape or likeness, except by the Creator Himself, Who made all things, is without doubt an infidel, and worse than a pagan.

And we will quote the arguments of S. Thomas in the 2nd Book of Sentences, VIII: Whether devils can affect the bodily sense by the delusion of a glamour. There he argues first that they cannot. For though that shape of a beast which is seen must be somewhere, it cannot exist only in the senses; for the sense perceive no shape that is not received from actual matter, and there is no actual beast there; and he adduces the authority of the Canon. And again, that which seems to be, cannot really be; as in the case of a woman who seems to be a beast, for two substantial shapes cannot exist at one and the same time in the same matter. Therefore, since that shape of a beast which appears cannot exist anywhere, no glamour or illusion can exist in the eye of the beholder; for the sight must have some object in which it terminates.

And if it is argued that the shape exists in the surrounding atmosphere, this is not possible; both because the atmosphere is not capable of taking any shape or form, and also because the air around that person is not always constant, and cannot be so on account of its fluid nature, especially when it is moved. And again because in that case such a transformation would be visible to everyone; but this is not so, because the devils seem to be unable to deceive the sight of Holy Men in the least.

Besides, the sense of sight, or the faculty of vision, is a passive faculty, and every passive faculty is set in motion by the active agent that corresponds to it. Now the active agent corresponding to sight is twofold: one is the origin of the act, or the object; the other is the carrier, or medium. But that apparent shape cannot be the object of the sense, neither can it be the medium through which it is carried. First, it cannot be the object, since it cannot be taken hold of by anything, as was shown in the foregoing argument, since it does not exist in the senses received from an object, neither is it in the actual object, nor even in the air, as in a carrying medium, as was treated of above in the third argument.

Besides, if the devil moves the inner consciousness, he does so either by projecting himself
[context] into the cognitive faculty, or by changing it.

# Solutions to the arguments.

The answer to the first is clear. There is no doubt that just as men can kill by God’s permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member or others. But in that case, the demons are not operating through the witches of whom mention is made here. And by this, the solution to the second also becomes clear. But as to the point that because God more broadly permits the generative power to be bewitched, etc., therefore it is also permitted that that member be truly and really removed, this argument does not hold, because this would not occur by way of witchcraft, nor do witches intend this when they perform such acts, as they do not have the power to restore the member whenever they wish and know. From this it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by prestigiosa arte.

Regarding the third, concerning the transformation of Lot’s wife, we say that it was real and not by the art of illusion; whereas here we are speaking of the art of illusion.

Regarding the fourth, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said regarding the magicians of Pharaoh that they created real serpents, and demons can produce certain effects regarding some imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do regarding humans, for whom God has greater care, according to that passage: "Does God care for oxen?" Nevertheless, as has been said, they can always, with God's permission, harm humans truly and really, or also by the art of illusion; and through this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

# Question X. Whether witches operate upon humans by transforming them into beastly forms through the art of illusion.

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared where they also transform humans into beasts. Regarding how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or into another appearance, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan. And let us use the arguments of Saint Thomas in his Second Book of Sentences, distinction 8: whether demons can imprint illusions upon the bodily senses. Where, firstly, he argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere, but it cannot exist only in the sense, because the sense does not have any species except that which is received from things, and there is no real beast there according to the cited canonical authority. Nor again can it be in the thing that is seen, such as when a woman appears to be a beast, because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same subject at the same time and at once. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen cannot be anywhere, no deceptive illusion can occur in the eye of the viewer, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that this form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be; firstly, because air is not receptive to any form or figure; and secondly, because the same air cannot remain around that person due to its fluidity, particularly when it moves. Thirdly, because such a transformation would be seen by everyone, which does not happen, since demons are not seen to deceive the visions of holy men at least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But everything passive is moved by an active agent proportioned to it. Now, the active agent proportioned to the sense is twofold: one as if originating the act, namely the object; the other as if referring, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor even the medium as if conveying it. But then demons do not act through the evil practices of which we have already spoken. And through this, the solution is also clear. But with regard to that, since God sends forth the generative power to cause evil, therefore also is it sent forth so that that limb may be truly and really removed. This does not hold, however, that this should always be done, because there would be no way for evil to take place, nor even when affected by evil, while such things are being done, and they do not have the power to restore the limb which they wish and know. From this it is clear that it is not truly removed, but is taken away by a magical art. With regard to the third, concerning the conversion of the wife, we say: it was true and not by magical art; now, however, we speak of magical art.
